speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not
intended to address the house on the South Saskatchewan river project at this time. I had thought that in all probability it would be discussed on my estimates, or at a time when the government was making some report with regard to the commission's report. However, an amendment has been moved to the motion to go into supply, and also an amendment to the amendment.
Some remarks have been made in discussing those amendments which make it necessary for me to make some comment. I would in the first place call the attention of hon. members to the fact that the amendment reads as follows:
I therefore move, seconded by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) -
And this was the amendment of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker):
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that in the estimates presented to this house no provision has been made for immediately proceeding with the construction of the South Saskatchewan river dam."
Well, there is a provision in the estimates for an expenditure similar to that of last year. There has been no decision reached as to whether the expenditure will be made. But the statement contained in the amendment is not a statement of fact; and therefore if members have no other reasons for voting against it, they certainly would vote against it on the ground that it is not a correct statement of fact.
In addition to that, an amendment to the amendment was moved in these words:
That the amendment be amended by adding at the end thereof the following words:
"as recommended by the federal government's P.F.R.A. engineers."
Well, the federal government's P.F.R.A. engineers have made no recommendation in connection with this matter whatsoever. It is not their mission. It is not their duty to make recommendations. They are asked for
1734	HOUSE OF
South Saskatchewan River Project reports on possible projects across western Canada, and any recommendations that are made are made here, by the minister, and not by P.F.R.A. engineers. So again I suggest that the amendment to the amendment is not based upon the facts as they exist, and therefore there could be no good reason for anyone voting either for the amendment or the amendment to the amendment. They are both statements of situations which do not exist.
But in view of the fact that amendments have been moved and that there have been discussions, and in view of the fact that for a long time the views of everyone who has been associated with public affairs in the province of Saskatchewan in particular, and in the western provinces in general, have been pretty well established, perhaps I should make' a few comments.
There is no necessity for me, on this occasion, to attempt to indicate to the house what my own views on this question are. I am on record in every session of the Saskatchewan legislature from 1916 until I came to this House of Commons in 1936; and that being the case, there would be no way of my avoiding that record which is known both to the newspapers of western Canada and to individuals concerned about the voting in western Canada. Anyone can look up the sessional papers and find out what position was taken over the years in relation to this particular question. All I am going to say at the moment is that on no occasion, at any time, either while an election was on or while an election was not on, have I stated that the South Saskatchewan river dam was going to be built.
I have on many occasions indicated that investigation is being made into the possibility of building it. I have on certain occasions indicated that, so far as I myself am concerned, I have been convinced that a dam can be built. But at no time has it been stated that the government has entered into any such arrangement or has undertaken to enter into any such arrangement. I intend to give the reasons as to why that is the case, as I go along.
I think in the first place I should perhaps give a very short review of what the history of the question has been. A short review would take me back a long time; but it does not require more than one sentence with regard to each matter in order to remind the house of what is involved historically in the discussion of this question.
Many years ago-as a matter of fact very shortly after confederation-a very definite


stand was taken with regard to land and resources in western Canada. The government of Sir John A. Macdonald took the position that we should follow the practice of the United States and make the land available to the railway companies in order to induce the construction of national railway lines across the Dominion of Canada. He followed that policy during tall the time he was in office, and made available something in the neighbourhood of 38 million acres, a very great part of which was taken from what is now the province of Saskatchewan- what was then the Northwest Territories-in order to encourage the building of national railways.
During that period of time the Liberal party took the position that this should not be done, that this was a national undertaking and that provision for that kind of thing should be made out of the treasury of Canada. When the Liberal party came into office in 1896 they changed the policy and determined upon a policy of making cash grants instead of land grants.
And so by 1904, as a result of that policy, they established the building of another line of railway from one end of Canada to the other, and in order to secure the building of that line they put up cash grants.
These are the two facts, away back at the beginning of the history, of this development which I think we have to keep in mind at this time. Then, in 1905, one year after the arrangement was made for the construction of this great national railway on the basis of cash grants, the government of the day set up two new provinces, the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. At that time they determined that while they were not going to make any more land grants to railways, and were not involving themselves in anything of that kind, that they were going to utilize the land of the western prairies, administered from Ottawa, for the purpose of encouraging settlement in the Dominion of Canada-the natural argument being that, the railways once having been constructed, and the great undertakings resulting having been developed from one end of Canada to the other, the lands should be retained rather than administered by the provinces. It was maintained at Ottawa that national problems could best be assisted if settlement were based on lands administered from Ottawa.
Well, settlement was carried out based on the previous areas and experiences from the beginning until 1908. It came about in 1908 that the area known as the Palliser triangle which had not been settled prior to that time-homesteading was not allowed in that

area, grants were not made to the railways in that area; settlement was discouraged, except for purposes of ranching, and grants of land were leased for ranching purposes over that area. In 1908 they decided to throw open these lands for settlement, not only settlement on the basis of homesteading, but the government of the day decided to sell 160-acre pre-emptions to any person who was homesteading in order to give him twice as much land as he would have under the policy which had been followed up to then.
I recite the details of these policies in order to show that up to that time there had been a very definite difference of opinion as between the two groups on different sides of this house. The Conservative party of that time had taken the position that making grants of land to the railroads was the proper thing to do, but when the new provinces were set up they took the position that the land should not be reserved to be administered from Ottawa, but should be administered by the provinces themselves. There was such wide division of policy on the part of the parties which resulted in the Conservative party in Saskatchewan changing its name to "provincial righters". As provincial righters they maintained that the lands and resources should be returned to the provinces and administered by the provinces.
As I said a moment ago, I have been associated with politics in the province of Saskatchewan ever since it was set up. During the early history of the province I took the position, along with other Liberals, that the proper thing to do was to have lands and resources administered by the provincial government, and more particularly prior to the period when it was decided to open up the Palliser triangle.
In 1912, just after a change of government, additions were made to three provinces in Canada, the province of Manitoba, the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec. That suggestion had been made prior to the change in government by the Laurier government of the day, but it was brought into being by the government of Sir Robert Borden. When it was brought into being it was provided that the resources of these areas would be turned over to the provinces.
They did not follow the practice which the government had followed previously of retaining the resources to be administered from Ottawa, but turned them over to those three provinces. From there on all the parties in western Canada took the position that, since the policy had been changed at Ottawa, the government should follow the
South Saskatchewan River Project same policy in connection with resources and lands of the prairie provinces.
Discussions with regard to this went on for some time and it was during the period from 1916 down to the time when I left Regina that I am on record fully with regard to my own position in connection with the whole matter. But in 1929, the then prime minister of Canada, the late Mr. King, made representations to the governments of the three prairie provinces to the effect that they had decided that the natural resources should be returned to the provinces.
I was then the premier of the province of Saskatchewan and I was a supporter of the Liberal party, both provincially and federally. When that offer was made to the government of the province of Saskatchewan I came to Ottawa, along with other members of the Saskatchewan government, and interviewed the government of the Dominion of Canada. They made certain proposals to us under which we were asked to take the control of the natural resources. We refused and we gave our reasons for refusing. We said that during the period when the lands and resources had been administered from Ottawa some 38 million acres of land had been alienated; that large areas of forests had been alienated; that large areas of mining property had been transferred to activities elsewhere and that in asking the provinces to administer the remnant we were being asked to maintain an organization in order to conserve forests which had been alienated and to take care of land which had been settled and much which in all probability would not be settled because it was the least acceptable. We contended that a great deal of expense would be involved.
So we said that the federal government should not only turn over the resources, they should turn over with them certain funds. The reaction of Mr. King to that suggestion was to appoint a royal commission. That royal commission was headed by the Hon. Alphonse Turgeon, then chief justice of the province of Saskatchewan. An election was held a few months later and Mr. King's government was defeated.
Mr. Bennett came into office and decided to continue the commission, but he continued it with a little different personnel. He removed Mr. Justice Turgeon and put in his place another judge, Mr. Justice Bigelow, who functioned on the commission. That commission sat for about four years and a half. By the time it reported we were back in office.

That is the history of what happened down to 1935 excepting that we had one of the worst depressions in Saskatchewan and western Canada from 1931 down to 1939 that had ever been experienced. I think everyone in western Canada, no matter to what party he belonged, and everyone who was associated with government in Canada became convinced by what had happened that there was something wrong with the methods under which that particular section of Canada known as the Palliser triangle had been settled.
I remember coming down to Ottawa after the change of government and suggesting to the prime minister of the day, the late Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, that the commitments which had been undertaken by the previous government should be met by Ottawa. During the discussions I was asked for an opinion as to whether I thought people would be able to live in that section of the country. Mr. Bennett naturally referred to the position he had taken in 1908 when he said that these lands should remain as lands occupied by ranchers who were producing cattle, that they should not be broken up.
But after we had discussed the matter for two days and called in representatives of the

When the Conservatives were in office in 1935 they brought in a bill. It was a short bill. It provided for the setting up of a committee. During the period when we were battling in the election campaign of 1935 we took certain attitudes with regard to this intention. South Saskatchewan River Project long ago that they were twitting me with having said that if the dam went out it would take the city of Saskatoon along with it. We had the experience last summer of a dam almost going out above Swift Current, and I had delegations down here wanting the government to pay for the houses that had been flooded, to pay for everything that happened in connection with it. Fortunately we were able to keep the dam in, but it could have gone out, and if it had gone out a very considerable part of Swift Current would have gone along with it. Therefore, I repeat, we are concerned about whether or not we can keep the dam there.
Having said that, I think you realize that I would have certainly been open to a great deal of criticism if I had appointed George Spence as chairman of this commission last year. I knew what George Spence would want to say without putting him on a commission. I know that he is the best P.F.R.A. official that we have had in western Canada.
I know that he is a member of the international joint commission. I know what his views are on the question. I do not need to ask it. As a matter of fact, he was the chairman of the board at the time that I was convinced you could build a dam on the South Saskatchewan river and therefore I have no reason to ask him. I knew too that he would make one of the best representations to the commission when it sat that would be made by anyone. I know George Spence well enough to know that he would do that, and he did it without being asked by me. Then I knew that if it was not satisfactory to him at the end he would make the best criticism of it that anyone has made, and he has done that and it is published in the press. If anyone wants to get the views of George Spence they can get them very easily by reading them. I know what his views are. But if I had appointed or recommended to the government that they appoint one or two men like George Spence on the commission, the commission would not have served the purpose which I had in my mind, nor would it have served the purpose that the government had in their minds. I was satisfied myself that a dam could be built there, but I have gone down underground since that time. I have walked through the tunnels that have been there. I have done that along with engineers and I have been told that the dam can be made to stay there. I have been told by three of the best consultants on the North American continent that the dam can be made to stay there, and after reading this report I am quite convinced that if at least two of the members of the commission had 

reported as they would like to have reported, they would have said that you could not build a dam there at all.
Who were the three?
Mr. Casagrande of Harvard, Mr. Harza, I think his name is, of Chicago, and General Ferguson, who has been a consultant in connection with it right along.
May I ask the minister what he means by "if they had been free to report as they would have wished to"?

No, I did not say "if they had been free to report as they wished to", but if they had reported as they probably thought when they were put on the commission they would have probably said no, it is pretty difficult to put it there. I am saying that because when they were appointed, as I said a moment ago, I was very careful in recommending it to the government not to recommend somebody who had preconceived ideas. As a matter of fact, when we were discussing the last man who went on the commission I made an inquiry of the government myself as to whether they were satisfied that the man did not have preconceived ideas with regard to it.
The reason I am pleased with the report of the commission is this: that feeling that having selected people who would have some reasons at least, or some inclination, to find in the opposite direction, they were unable to say after they investigated the whole project that it cannot be built there.
Now, I was reading from a good editorial -I almost feel like reading it to the house- in the Albertan, which was quite critical of this whole project prior to the time the commission was set up, and which has now written an editorial which I think is quite characteristic of the editorials that have been written in western Canada. I think I ought to read part, if not all, of it. They say this:
Right after the war the federal government started talking about a large irrigation project on the South Saskatchewan river somewhere in Saskatchewan. The government's efficient prairie farm rehabilitation administration staff went to work on the idea, found a suitable site, drew plans and pursued all the other preliminary tasks. The provincial government agreed to assume a good deal of the cost. As this had long been a favourite policy of Mr. Gardiner, what was there to stand in the way?
Then they go on to say this:
Then something over a year ago Ottawa decided to have a royal commission look into the advisability of the project. This seemed to many people to be just a stall, but, as the Albertan said then, if there is any doubt about the economic feasibility of the project, it's better to find out now than after the thing is built.

The commission, consisting of three competent engineers, made an exhaustive survey and about three months ago completed its report. But well before it was written, one commission member-
I do not know which one this was, but it gives me reason for what I said a moment ago.
-dropped the hint that the report would advise against the project. Shortly after the report was signed, the word leaked out that that was so. Thus, before the official disclosure of the contents, there has been a general controversy on the findings of the commission. Mr. Gardiner, the P.F.R.A. and many other people have been quite critical. Saskatchewan is quite disillusioned. And now, in the midst of this debate, the report is released. For the first time the public knows exactly what is in it.
As for us. we find it a mixture of good and bad.
Among the points that needed saying by someone with the authority of this commission, and which cannot be disputed or minimized, are these:
I am not going to read them all. Perhaps I should read the first one, just to indicate what it is about:
1.	Markets are a first consideration. Irrigation means very specialized farming, and that means new crops and new crops mean new markets.
All I will say about that is that it will be ten years before the dam is completed, and it will be at least five years after that before enough land is irrigated to make much difference. Fifteen years is a long time to be preparing markets. No one can say at this time what the market will be. But I would not put as much emphasis upon markets as they are putting upon them at the moment. Nevertheless the report did put some emphasis upon the matter, and they make reference to it.
Then the editorial goes on:
2.	There ought to be an over-all approach to the question of river development in the three prairie provinces. This is not something for haphazard growth. The various legal and engineering problems ought to be worked out now, with Ottawa taking the lead although the provinces are in actual control of the rivers. Diversion of the North Saskatchewan to the South Saskatchewan, and the Athabasca and Churchill to the North Saskatchewan, are matters which, if investigated now, might put a different light on the whole matter.
All I wish to say is that P.F.R.A., or myself, through Justice, have entered into all the questions which are referred to here; and we are quite satisfied in view of the fact that these are matters which are the responsibility of the provinces, and not the responsibility of the federal government-ever since the natural resources were returned to the provinces, and since we are simply engaged in the task of handing the provinces something which we think they are entitled to, because we did not make as good a job of settling the lands as we should have made while they were under our administration.
South Saskatchewan River Project
We say that we are prepared to give them something. One of the things we have already given Alberta is the St. Mary dam. One we are in process of giving them is the Bow river project. One we are considering whether or not we will give them is the Red Deer project. One we are considering in Saskatchewan, as to whether or not we will pay for it, is the South Saskatchewan river project.
Now, all you need to do is to take the correspondence at the tail end of the report and read it. If you do you will find that this question has been under discussion ever since these larger projects were first considered. The provinces themselves, under Mr. Bracken's leadership, set up a water board. That water board was going to determine what was going to happen in the different provinces, irrespective of what the federal government did. Two years later it was converted into a board on which the federal government had representation, the chief reason being that the federal government indicated that we were not going to get into any controversy with the provinces of western Canada as to what should be done with water in Alberta in order to transfer it into Saskatchewan. We were not going to get into any difficulty, so we joined in setting up the board, and that board is there. They have the power, the authority and the information upon which to base decision on all these questions raised here.
Then the editorial continues:
3.	Irrigation ought to go ahead, in different ways if not in this way.
That is their opinion, I know, but I think everyone here agrees with them.
Of great interest to Alberta is the apparent approval given to the Red Deer diversion scheme which would irrigate half a million acres in east-central Alberta and which, the commission suggests, might be taken well into Saskatchewan.
We have never raised any objection to taking water into Saskatchewan out of Alberta. We have never suggested whether it should be or should not be done because, after all, it is a matter to be determined between the provinces. We have said that if Alberta wants to provide water in the Sullivan dam, or somewhere else, that can be utilized across the line in Saskatchewan, that province should make an agreement with the Alberta government-and it should be done without controversy at all. We are not going to step into the picture at all and tell either of them that they should or should not do certain things.
That is something which we say should be determined as between the provinces, before we are brought into the picture at all. And so we have suggested that they ought to take
1744	HOUSE OF
South Saskatchewan River Project those matters to the water board and have them settled. After they are settled, we will be in a position to go and talk to them about the other features of the South Saskatchewan. Then they go on to say this:
And among the points with which we take issue are the following:
That is, they are referring to the points raised in the commission's report. Then the other points are included. It goes on to say that, among others, the first of these is the estimated cost. I am not going to go into that matter at all. I think it would be better to do so at some other time. However, they do deal with the matter and give reasons for believing why the cost should not be anything like the amount mentioned.
Then they make reference to the size of farming units, and show a statement in that connection-that they do not carry out the experience that has been had at the St. Mary dam or the Bow river dam, and I am inclined to agree with them on that.
Then they go on to refer to the rights of the other provinces, and say:
The commission seems unduly concerned about objections of Alberta and Manitoba, for, after all, it says, the river belongs to them too. But Alberta before long will be watering close to a million acres from the tributaries of the South Saskatchewan, and Manitoba's fears of losing water power potential are hardly well grounded, with so many other sites available and new water diversion from other watersheds distinctly possible.
Then they just ask this question: What about Saskatchewan's rights? I say again that that is a very fair editorial coming from the province of Alberta. The only objections that have come to this proposal have come from Alberta. I have read the report most carefully and I cannot find that a single individual who appeared before that commission, excepting one engineer from Alberta, raised objection. I think those who base their decisions on that objection ought to go back and look up the records. I am not going to recite them to you today because they are all on record. I have no doubt that some of my friends from Alberta know what the record is.

The minister has told us of the difficulties in Alberta and a while ago they made the statement, "We are not in position now to go ahead with the South Saskatchewan river dam." He did not use the word "project". Is it because of the attitude of Alberta that the minister made that statement?

No, if I made that statement- Mr. Diefenbaker: Those are the exact words. Mr. Gardiner: I can imagine that a great deal was said before and after it if I said 

that. In any case, if I did, it simply meant that we have not yet made our decision on the question. We have not yet discussed it with the province of Saskatchewan since the report is out, and until it is discussed we are not in position to proceed.
Or with the cabinet?

Or with the cabinet. It has not been discussed at either place. I want it distinctly understood that there is not any trouble between myself and any other member of the government. There has never been any trouble about who was going to be on the commission. The government accepted the commission which I recommended. My chief reason for recommending someone that I was not definitely sure was going to say that you could build a dam was that we should be certain before undertaking the construction that the dam would not go out and take Saskatoon with it. When I found a commission, of the kind which was appointed, not in position to say that there was any danger in building the dam, in so far as my own feelings in the matter are concerned I think I was strengthened. My own views are strengthened by the report of the commission rather than otherwise.
You whispered it to other members of the government.

I not only whispered it, I said it out loud. This is a matter we are trying to reach a reasonable decision about in the hope that if it is done we will be doing something which is in the interests, not only of the area itself but of all Canada, and that the money, if expended, is going to be well expended on a project of that kind.

Just with the idea of clarifying the statement the minister has made, I would ask the minister to clarify what he said about this never having been discussed in the cabinet. Was it not discussed in the cabinet before the commission was appointed to make an inquiry into this matter?

Not the question of whether we were going to do it. As a matter of fact, the only time that this project as such was discussed was on each occasion when we voted money to investigate it. That has been done every year since 1949-50. There have been definite votes. There was a vote of $7,500,000 the first year and $7,890,000 the last year for large projects. Part of that money was set aside for expenditure on the South Saskatchewan. There is still money in the estimates this year for that purpose. Every year that that was brought up I discussed my estimates with the treasury board and with

council and I always submitted an argument in favour of going ahead and making this investigation. Every year the government agreed that the money should be spent in that way and it has been spent in that way.
Coming down to May 31, 1951, I think it was-this	is indicated in Hansard-I
announced the government's position in relation to it, that they were going to appoint a commission. I repeat now that when I brought the recommendation in, that the matter be discussed with the Saskatchewan government, the Prime Minister said to me-
I hope you will not consider this a matter as revealing something that happened in council-
You mean the Prime Minister of Canada?

He just said to me, "Have you any objection to the matter being referred to a commissioner or commissioners?" That suggestion was made in the light of some of the reports that had been made to us, and some other things. I was asked if I had any objection to there being a commission, and I said, "No, I have not". That was the discussion. I came into the house that evening and I reported-this is on the record-and two or three days later I recommended a commission. That commission was accepted by the government. They saw the individuals; two of them accepted and one could not. We went on and finally got the commission set up, and the commission reported.
The commission reported, as you know, on January 12. From that time to this there have been no discussions of it. We have not had an opportunity of discussing it and it has not been discussed up to now. That is the present position.
Do I understand the minister to say that he never at any time made a recommendation to the cabinet that the South Saskatchewan river project should be given consideration by the government?

I did not say that I had never recommended it be given consideration. I said I had never yet been in position to recommend that it be proceeded with. The reason for that is an order in council, I think it is 2298 of 1947, which definitely states the procedure that must be followed in the case of every large project. Large projects are not built by P.F.R.A., they are carried out as individual jobs or projects. When it comes to the matter of building a dam in Saskatchewan, that is an individual project that will have to be brought up under that order in council.
South Saskatchewan River Project
Under that order in council I came to the government on May 30, 1951, and stated that I thought the matter was in a position where it could be discussed with the Saskatchewan government and I recommended that it be discussed. When it reached that stage they appointed a commission, and it is in that stage yet. The recommendation now would be, not that we proceed with the dam immediately but that we proceed with the discussion with the Saskatchewan government. That would be the proper procedure and it is the one that would be followed if the decision was arrived at to proceed with further discussion.
The Saskatchewan government is now in a position where they know everything that has been represented to us. We know everything that has been represented to them. When the government has given consideration to it, it will be with all those facts before them. If I am directed to go to Regina and discuss the matter with the Saskatchewan government it will be with all those facts before us.
In other words, you have never yet discussed it with the Saskatchewan government?

No, not since 1951, which I think was the last discussion we had with them. In 1950 we discussed it with them and they were not too sure at that time just what they wanted to do. But a few months later they were fairly sure that they wanted to proceed; in fact I think they have been sure that they wanted to proceed since that time, after having had a discussion with us.
That is the position in relation to it. I thought it better that hon. members should know the position as we see it. I will just summarize what I have been saying in this way. The South Saskatchewan river project, so far as we are concerned, is the dam.
What does the minister mean by "we"?
I mean the government. We have never considered anything else, doing anything else but building the dam and putting in the reservoir.
That is not the government because you have not spoken to the cabinet about it.

From the beginning when we started to talk about the project as such. I would not just come out and say today, "I am going to recommend this." We have been working on this for ten years. All I am saying is that we have had money voted by the government to work on it. At the end

South Saskatchewan River Project of that ten years I am in a position to say that I think this project is on all fours with the St. Mary and Bow river projects with only one difference, namely, that it will cost considerably more money than the other two. I think we ought to discuss it with the Saskatchewan government. It has got to that stage.
How did these items get in the estimates without being discussed by the government?
There are many items put in the estimates without a decision being made that the job is going to be done this year.
Window-dressing.

I should like to recall to my hon. friend's mind that I believe there was an item put in the estimates to build a post office in one of the Saskatchewan constituencies away back in the time of Mr. Bennett, and I think it was built last year. The fact that these items go into the estimates should not suggest that you are going to do it next week.
Would the minister allow a question?
I would say that the South Saskatchewan project, as far as we are concerned-

Would the minister allow a question in connection with the estimates? Is the item that is provided in the estimates this year for the construction of the dam or merely for preliminary work as in the past?

I must say this because I will probably be saying it when I come to the estimates and I had better say it now. Sometimes mistakes are made in even putting items in the estimates, and in so far as this particular matter is concerned $500,000 is just as good as $1 million; but when that estimate was placed before treasury board-my hon. friend smiles at that. The fact is that there is an estimate there while the amendment says that there is not.
It says for construction of the dam.
So far as the amount of $1 million is concerned, which is the amount that is supposed to be there-and it can be adjusted to put it there-
For construction.
-if we once decide to construct the dam I doubt very much if you can spend any more than $1 million on construction in the first year.
Is that what the $1 million is there for, construction?
If we once decide to do it, it is.
That is not what it says.

It could be utilized for that purpose. In the second place, the dam would be the final act of rehabilitation in Saskatchewan. We started out to rehabilitate the areas that had not been properly settled. We said we would spend a considerable amount of money on it. By the time we get through with this we will have spent from $7.50 to $10 an acre on every acre of land utilized for this purpose, and that is quite a bit of money. What we have suggested is that all activities and expenditures will at some time or other revert to the province. Our position will be that we have rehabilitated the area and have put it in the same position in relation to Ottawa as every other province, and therefore it is the province's job to go ahead and continue from there.
The only four projects in western Canada that have been proposed on that basis are the four I have mentioned. The only other one which is even similar is the one involving the Assiniboine river in the province of Manitoba where we have been making surveys near the boundary line between the two provinces. When rehabilitation is fully planned and finally under way, an act generally applicable to all provinces based upon benefits to agriculture should replace the present P.F.R.A. legislation. I think we have discussed the possibilities of that every year now for the last three years, and I would say again that, in view of the change in attitude toward expenditures, provincially and federally, there will be good reason when we draw toward the end of real rehabilitation work to have an act based upon our experience in that area which can be applied in different parts of Canada to take care of soil surveys and other activities in connection with the improvement of farm lands across Canada.
We feel that if there are differences among the three western provinces with respect to the utilization of the water in the Saskatchewan river basin they should meet under the waters board and remove these objections, whatever they are, before we discuss the matter with them or we will not be able to arrive at very definite conclusions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Would the minister permit a question? Can he say whom he refers to in his use of "we" in this prepared part of his statement?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: He has already answered that.
I am referring to myself and other members of the government-the government of Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Does the minister mean the members of the government with whom he has not discussed the matter?
I think I know them as well as my hon. friend does.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: But the minister says he has not discussed the question with them at all.
I have a pretty good idea what they think about most of the matters I am talking about in spite of the fact we have not discussed them.
A one-man cabinet.

My recommendation has been and my recommendation still is that these two projects, the Red Deer and the South Saskatchewan, be discussed to a final conclusion and that that conclusion be taken up with the two provinces and finally determined upon. That is our intention, and I am not in a position to go any further than that at the moment. I would suggest that I do not see any good point in continuing the amendment to the motion to go into supply in view of the fact that it does not indicate the facts as they are and in view of the fact that I think all members from western Canada will be pretty well agreed on what should be done about the South Saskatchewan river dam. I am not so sure that all members from all parts of Canada would not be agreed. Why put members in the position of having to vote against the amendment just because it contains statements that are not correct or just because, if it should be passed, it would be interpreted by some people at least as a vote of want of confidence in the government? Why should they insist on that? The objective of all of us is to try to set up conditions under which this project will be carried through, and I think the sooner we get down to the estimates and get talking about something when we have decisions made the better it will be for all of us. I would therefore suggest that we drop this discussion and go on to something else. I hope my friends will agree with that for the moment, and then we can finish this discussion at the proper time when we have all the information before us.

Mr. Speaker, after listening to the minister's very interesting hour and a half speech on the South Saskatchewan dam project I B8108-112
South Saskatchewan River Project am afraid I am no more convinced now than I was before he started that the people of Saskatchewan are receiving a fair deal with respect to the project. In fact, I am becoming more and more convinced that they are not.
Who cares what you think?

This afternoon the minister discussed practically everything else except the reason why the government has not proceeded long ago with the project which he has been promising the people of Saskatchewan for a long time. This afternoon the minister said that he had not been promising this dam. I should like to read a quotation from the Regina Leader-Post dealing with a speech that the minister made at a luncheon gathering of the Regina board of trade on April 27, 1946. The report reads as follows:
The dominion government had already mapped out a program, and it was a program involving $110 million. This would be used largely in providing for the storage of water and partly for the distribution of this water where needed. The dominion government thus did not need the endorsation of the South Saskatchewan river development association to begin work on the South Saskatchewan river. It had already decided to go through with it.
The article reports the minister as going on to say:
-a decision would be reached on where the dam on the South Saskatchewan should be placed. It would be on one of three sites between the Elbow and Saskatoon. As soon as the site had been finally decided upon contracts would be let, and work would proceed immediately.
That is seven years ago. Well, listening to the minister's speech this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I was reminded very much of the speeches we have become used to from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) because we took a cross-country tour and we arrived absolutely nowhere.
We learned only two things: first of all that the matter has never been discussed in the cabinet, and the probability is that it will not be discussed for an indefinite period of time; and the second, a most interesting thing, and these are the minister's own words because I jotted them down as he spoke, "the commissioners were not free to report as they would have desired". That I think is a very interesting thing to have learned.
Of their own choice.
Well, I jotted that down.

There was an explanation given. I do not think my hon. friend wants to be fair. I was asked about it at the time I made the statement. I explained what I meant and I think that is what should be stated now.

South Saskatchewan River Project

Well, Mr. Speaker, it has convinced me that the commissioners were not reporting as, in all probability, they would have liked to report. That is the impression that has been left with me.
Now, the minister told us that the cabinet would like to reach a reasonable decision upon this matter, but I want to ask him how in the world we are ever going to get anybody to reach a reasonable decision on anything if they refuse to discuss it. He told us that this thing is probably not going to be discussed for an indefinite period of time. I would like to know how this thing is ever going to be approved unless the cabinet is going to come to grips with it. From what I can see, they just want to promise it for the next election and then put it off, promise it again and put it off-just to keep the old evergreen tree in the forest ever growing.
They are going to be here a long time.
If these promises are not going to be kept you will not be here after the next election.
You said so yourself.
I said you people could promise them-and you can promise them just as well in opposition. You do not have to be in government to promise them. You can do that in opposition.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

We will give them four more weeks. Now, Mr. Speaker, after studying this South Saskatchewan project report, I have been left with the very definite impression that the commissioners must have received a directive from this government to bring in a report proving that this dam should not be built. I come to that conclusion because practically no attention has been paid to the great number of benefits that would derive from this project, and all attention seems to have been concentrated on the few drawbacks. So, I am left with that impression, and it is a very disturbing impression to receive when there had been expected a free commission with tremendous experience which could have been expected to bring in a report that one could really rely upon.
Another thing the minister said this afternoon was that the people in Alberta had no concern whether this project was built or not. That is a statement I wish to disagree with very heartily and I want to say that this project is not only of importance to the people of Saskatchewan but it is of prime importance to all of the people of this country.

Might I just say, as a matter of keeping the record straight, that what I said about Alberta I read from an editorial published by the Calgary Albertan in the city of Calgary. I do not think even that meant just exactly what my friend has indicated.
I was not trying to misinterpret the minister's words but I understood the minister to say that he agreed with the editorial, that is all.
I did, but the editorial does not say that.

As a resident of Ontario, Mr. Speaker, I have learned that the prosperity of Ontario depends very largely on the prosperity of all other parts of the country. We, in central Canada, have learned that we cannot be prosperous unless the west and the maritimes are prosperous as well. So, I feel that statement about other provinces not being interested in this project is a completely erroneous one.
Who made that statement?
It was a statement made in the paper and I understand and still believe that the minister agrees with it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The hon. member must take the minister's word for what his statement was. The minister stood up a minute ago and explained what he did not agree with and told what he agreed with 

and so the hon. member must accept the minister's word for it.

I did not understand the minister to say he disagreed. I thought he said they were not his words but that he was reading from an editorial.
In addition to providing much-needed irrigation for the farm lands of Saskatchewan, one of the things that appeal to me, as someone coming from central Canada, is the fact that this project would provide very important sources of hydroelectric power for the people of Saskatchewan, and would make it possible to bring industries to that province to make their economy less dependent on agriculture.
I believe that if we are going to build a stable economy in this country, we must make it possible for industries to move to the prairie provinces and to the maritimes. That cannot be done unless provision is made for hydroelectric power. That is the first step, and I believe that this project is an ideal example of just how that can be done.
I believe that this is the kind of project that can only be undertaken by government, because of its size. I believe that this is the

kind of project that government should undertake, and it is for that reason I strongly urge this government to go ahead with the project.
I believe that they will be doing a great service, not only to the people of Saskatchewan, but to all of the people of this country. I believe that it will be a very forward step in making possible diversification of industry right across this nation. That is a most necessary step if we are to arrive at a really stable economy.
I was out in Saskatchewan a year ago and I talked to a great many people who would be affected by this project. I was first of all very much impressed by the stories they told me of conditions that existed in the area during the thirties. I was amazed that conditions could be so bad and last for so long. I was also very much impressed by the fervent hope that had been engendered in these people by what they considered to be the firm promise by this government that this dam would be built. The minister has said that he has not promised that the dam would be built; but he has certainly created an impression in the minds of the people of Saskatchewan that this government would proceed with this project. I appeal to him on grounds of political honesty, if nothing else, because in some way or another the people in that area have been convinced that this government is going ahead with this project. I urge him on that ground, if nothing else, to do everything that he can to persuade his colleagues that it should be undertaken, when they finally get around to discussing this project.
Tell them about it anyway.
Yes, tell them about it. Discuss it back and forth. I urge the minister and the other members of the government to go ahead with this project at the very earliest possible opportunity.
As a speech the minister's was a fine statement. He talked for some hour and a half but I am not sure that he had sufficient time to make himself too clear.
I might say that if I had not been asked any questions I would have got through in an hour and made it clear.

I am not interested in the history of the past. At the moment I am interested in what the forecast is for the future.
The minister did give us, although he did not need to give it to us, his own personal view that he is in favour of the building of the dam. We have known that for many years since he has made it the basis of many election promises and the minister knows that is true.

South Saskatchewan River Project
He said, in the course of his speech, that he had never said the dam would be built. He could not say that without cabinet consent, but he did promise it in the political sense-and the minister need not shake his head at me. I heard him at the technical school in Saskatoon-he promised $110 million of expenditure of federal money on the undertaking, if we may call it that, the next year. I know there was certain mention of Alberta, but I also know that at that time the Saskatchewan project was supposed to cost only $65 million, and I know that in the minds of his listeners and in the press- because I have the clipping-$110 million was promised.

As a matter of privilege, Mr. Speaker, may I say this. Reference has been made twice, both by the hon. member who preceded him and by the hon. member who is now speaking, to an expenditure of $110 million. That expenditure which was under discussion for some years was an expenditure that was reported here to the committee of this house in 1943 and it was $110 million covering all four of these projects. We know now that it is much bigger than that.

Exactly. It covered those four projects. It included building the South Saskatchewan dam, in those days a project the estimate for which was much less than at present. Certainly we had the conviction that that amount of money at that time would have covered it, whether that was right or wrong.
I took down a note or two of some of the minister's remarks today and I might deal with these first. He expressed his personal view, but at that particular time I had the impression here that he was not expressing the view of the government. He did that later. He was asked about the word "we", and I will come to that matter later. But he did not give us any decision as to action or inaction as the result of this report. I propose to keep to the subject in spite of the smoke screen that was laid down by the minister, as he is so capable of doing. I remember what happened once before when I twitted him-if that is the right word-on this particular matter. The minister has a habit, when you ask him question A, of going to question B; and as the former member for Cariboo said at the time, then we are all at "C". As a matter of fact that has been the situation in so far as the people of Saskatchewan are concerned ever since 1943, when the minister started this campaign-a campaign, may I say, of various kinds.
I believe in taking the minister at his word, but my word is also of some value. I know what I heard him say on the radio

South Saskatchewan River Project and I have seen him quoted by men whom I consider to be good reporters. I know they can make mistakes; they have made some with reference to myself. The minister says this-I was amazed at this statement-and I wrote it down as he said it: "P.F.R.A. is not associated with the building of the dam". We know it is not the job of P.F.R.A. to build the dam, but I should like to have the minister check the figures. I might say to him that when he gives 1946 or 1947 as the date of any survey into this matter, it goes back further than that. In the sessional paper No. 170B of Tuesday, February 3, I asked the question:
What was the total amount spent by P.F.R.A., since and including 1942 to the present date,

And then note the words:
-upon studies or surveys of the South Saskatchewan river project.
The question is clear enough. Then we have the answer. We have a total expenditure, for the years for which I asked, of $2,780,489. I am going to suggest to the minister that that is a great deal of money to spend on a survey for one project and that it must have resulted in the accumulation of a good deal of expert knowledge with regard to that particular project.

Would my hon. friend allow me to answer the question he raises? This report says that the money was spent out of P.F.R.A. funds down to 1948-49. Some money was spent under P.F.R.A. each year during the period when we were investigating the possibilities of building a dam somewhere in Saskatchewan. When the location was determined, from there on it was $869,000 in 1949-50 and large sums after that, not taken out of P.F.R.A. but out of the major projects vote.

I think my question was fairly specific and that I obtained a reasonably specific answer. My interpretation of that answer is that P.F.R.A. spent almost $3 million specifically on surveys into the practicability of building what is known as the South Saskatchewan dam.
The next thing I come to is the part where the minister says the matter has never been discussed in the dominion cabinet. I have always admired the minister as a missionary for this project before the cabinet. I can only say I am disappointed that the matter has never been brought before that body. The situation looks bad. I would suggest that it does not look as though the minister had any particular faith in his colleagues, or else it looks as though his colleagues have no particular faith in him. Yet later he uses the term "we"; and in reply to a


question he said that that "we" referred to himself and his colleagues in the cabinet.
I was interested to know that the members of the commission had been appointed by the Minister of Agriculture himself. Then I was astonished at the following statement; I am not sure that I picked it up properly. Apparently he was pleased with this report because, forsooth, it finds in the opposite direction from his own personal favourable opinion.
Oh, no.
That is as I understood what the minister said.

If the hon. member wishes to be clear on that point may I say that what I said was the very opposite. I said the fact I was concerned about was whether a dam could be made to stay at that location. They have not said that it could not be made to stay there, a fact which has justified me in thinking it can stay there.

I thank the minister. The next statement I come to is the statement that there had not actually been any discussion with the province of Saskatchewan. That also is an amazing thing to me in view of the correspondence, copies of which I have here, between Premier Douglas and, may I say, the minister himself. It is dated 1951. I might quote a line or two from it. This is from Premier Douglas and he is addressing the Minister of Agriculture:
My colleagues and I are most anxious that the * South Saskatchewan river development project shall be proceeded with at the earliest possible date. As soon as the federal government has announced its intention-
If there has been no discussion, I suggest that it would be difficult for them to announce the intention.
-to proceed with this undertaking we are prepared to negotiate and sign an agreement on the basis of the allocation of costs outlined above.
Just in case we might not be sure that the minister had received that communication, here is the answer to it written by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to Hon. T. C. Douglas:
I note that as soon as the federal government has announced its intention to proceed with this undertaking your government is prepared to negotiate and sign an agreement on the basis of the above allocation of costs.
Mr. Douglas said in a letter following:
In view of the foregoing, we cannot see that any further delay is necessary. We would urge again that the government of Canada should recognize its obligations in this matter and undertake the immediate construction of this project which will undoubtedly benefit the nation as a whole and Saskatchewan in particular.

My own idea about this commission being set up was this. I did not see any necessity for a commission at all. I was basing that view on the fact that if $3 million had been spent by competent engineers solely on the study and survey of this particular question, then everything that could be said had been said. I suggest that is the reason the people of Saskatchewan got the idea that this was simply another stall to put the matter off for a year in order to give the minister time to bring the matter before the dominion cabinet for discussion. At any rate the letter continues:
Dr. L. B. Thomson has in fact expressed to us-
Again this is a letter from the premier to the Minister of Agriculture.
-the view that no irrigation project in Canada has ever been so thoroughly and carefully documented as this proposal.
Mr. Douglas says:
We cannot appreciate the need for this further review, but are of course prepared to co-operate with the committee in any way we possibly can expedite their work.
That seems a reasonable position to take. Now that we have finished the discussion with the minister, the main thing is that we have to keep our eye on the ball. If I may use the vernacular, the main thing is, where do we go from here? What is the prospect for the future? Judging by the minister's statement today, I would think it is not very bright. He has been talking of ten years, fifteen years and so on. Of course he has this justification, that we have been ten years or fifteen years in the past and that again can be translated in terms of another ten years or fifteen years in the future.
As I see it, the main thing we have to concern ourselves with is that the report of the commission on this project has been unfavourable. Like other towns in the district, we in the city of Saskatoon are terribly disappointed. We are progressing in that town. Things have been progressing. We will be getting natural gas next year. It would seem that electric power will be cheaper there in the future. We had hoped that this project would have increased the population of the surrounding area, would have increased and made more profitable business in the city, and that we might have had a beginning of heavy industry owing to the fact that power would have been abundant and that more local markets would be available. Therefore I do not think anyone there or in the surrounding territory will accept this decision of the commissioners as final. We think there should be a further investigation before this matter is completely written off.
South Saskatchewan River Project
Previous speakers have opened wide and deep holes in the report itself. I shall not do that. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), among others, took the report paragraph by paragraph and gave it some criticism.
There were two circumstances particularly conducive to an unfavourable report. One of these was the fact that the district, as the minister well knows, has for the last two years enjoyed a much better rainfall than it had throughout the previous years. That is to say, the commission held its sittings after two of the most prosperous years, in the matter of wheat crops owing to extra precipitation, that we have had in our history. If that report had been written by men who were sitting in a hotel room full of dust, with dust all over their tables, dust on their floors and wind howling outside the window, I fancy the report would have had a different complexion. If it had been written in the year 1936 or 1937 it would have been different. The other unfortunate thing is the death of Dr. Widtsoe who, as I see it, was really the only irrigation man on that commission, because I understand the other men can be classified as power engineers. They were interested chiefly in the potential production of power from that project.
Well, we must not allow a red herring to be drawn across the trail. By the term "red herring" I refer to these counter-proposals, most of which I think would favour the province of Alberta. Alberta has already benefited from any irrigation work the dominion government has undertaken. I came across an editorial in the Leader-Post which says:
Up to now, condemnation of the report has been unanimous, in Saskatchewan at least, although a contrary note has been sounded in Alberta where that government's minister of agriculture expressed gratitude to the commission and declared, in effect, that its recommendations were exactly what the neighbouring province wanted.
I do not know whether that is the statement to which the minister referred when he said he could hardly believe that the man meant to say what he was apparently reported as having said, and I share that feeling with him because I do not think Alberta, which has nothing to lose in this particular matter, would give this as their considered opinion about a thing which would so benefit the population of a neighbouring province.
These other things of course are only supplementary. They are not substitutes for the main project. The main objection to the project in the report is the cost. I think the estimated cost was $247 million, and I believe they raised that to $250 million. A great
1752	HOUSE OF
South Saskatchewan River Project many other people do not accept that figure. It is about twice as great as the estimate of the P.F.R.A. engineers, and I do not believe their estimate was given very much before this one in point of time. We have always wondered why the P.F.R.A. engineers were not given an opportunity to come before the commission to say whatever they had in their minds. We think the government was in some way or other opposed to its own engineers and officials going to the place where they might give opinions favourable to the project.
May I repeat what I said the other day. These men were available to the commission at all times, and the commission did see them about all these matters.
Not in a public hearing.
Well, that is not necessary; they saw them and had their opinions.

That may be so, but they certainly were not called before a public hearing.
As to the talk that this great expenditure is not justified in the national interest, well, it is apparently in the national interest to spend a billion dollars on the St. Lawrence seaway in the east. We in the west are not opposed to that. I am sure none of our western members has opposed it, or I have not heard of any of them opposing it. If it is for the good of Canada, they are for it. If the government is prepared to spend that much money in eastern Canada in the national interest, we also claim some share of the national purse in the national interest, and we do believe that this project would be in the national interest. That the provincial government has guaranteed to do its share has been amply proven. I am not going to read the correspondence; it is all on record. I think it has been put on the record earlier in this debate. I refer to letters from Premier Douglas.
After the 1949 election, when the Minister of Agriculture came back and told us so blandly that we could not do anything without the consent of the province, I think Premier Douglas sent either a letter or a telegram to the minister assuring the minister of that province's co-operation. And in the face of changed circumstances, even if the cost in this report were accepted, there is the record of the correspondence between Premier Douglas and the minister in which the premier again, in spite of the raised estimate, assured the minister of his co-operation in that regard. I think the correspondence was put on the record by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright). I am not going to touch on it today.


I have said that the P.F.R.A. officials had valuable evidence which they could have submitted had they been asked for it at a public hearing. We do not know what they said privately to these engineers. We are not interested, because this is public business and public business must be a matter of record. I suggest that these are men who know something about the thing they are doing. The minister will agree with that, and furthermore these men have lived with it. I do not mean that metaphorically; I mean it literally. They have lived there in Saskatchewan doing their work. They understand the conditions. A lot of them have lived there during the dry years. They made extensive studies. As I have said, a large amount of money has been spent on these studies. The amount spent on studies and surveys was $2,780,489. I suggest that when the commission was set up, to a great extent the facts were already known. I have already quoted Mr. Thomson's remark in that regard.
Now, I am not going to suggest that these latter surveys, the ones that I do not think were particularly necessary, were made purely for political reasons. But I do say that their outward manifestation certainly did not do any harm to the Liberal party in Saskatchewan throughout those years. People who see these engineers with their cars and1 bulldozers working along the river bank will say, "This government is really going to do something".
As a matter of fact I have come to be just a little bit political. As I say, I think the whole political history of the thing has been somewhat unsavoury. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has done much to promote this idea and, more than that, to popularize it in the public mind. Presumably this is done in the interests of the nation, but if a little popular favour happens to fall his way or to his side, and he can garner a few votes, that is all to the good, of course.
We do not blame him for that, so long as he fulfils the promises he makes. In 1944 the vast sums to which I have referred were promised; I have heard the minister make reference to them, myself. Then in 1945, before the election, it was exactly the same thing. Then came the by-election in Rosthern. I believe it was in 1948, when the junior member for Rosthern (Mr. Boucher) was elected. We had maps-do you remember the maps in the Star-Phoenix, and in other papers?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I took part in it.
With all due respect to the minister, I would just as soon trust the memory of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: All right; but if you want the truth I will give it to you.
If you want the truth, go to Paul.

I do not know whether the minister perpetrated the material put out by our Liberal friends at that time, but everybody knows that the Rosthern area is for the most part away up north of Saskatoon, and would not be affected by this project. But they have lakes and rivers all over that map.
It is the same map that is in here.

Then on October 20, 1948, the then member for Rosthern, Mr. Tucker, said, "It is up to the people of Rosthern to give their endorsation to Mr. Boucher, the Liberal candidate, if they want the project proceeded with".

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit an interruption?
Is the minister objecting to what I am saying?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: No. I want to correct what I said a moment ago. For the first time in many weeks the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was right.
And Paul was wrong. Well, what do you know about that?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: As the minister knows, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is always right.

I am going to suggest that there is a threat in what was said by Mr. Tucker at that time-"if they want the project proceeded with". There were lots of statements. It was a subtle sort of thing, with references to the necessity of a more co-operative government in Saskatchewan. There was a suggestion, for instance, that if we had a government in Saskatchewan of the same political complexion as the federal government, it would be much simpler to get these things done. Then Mr. Boucher came to Ottawa; and I now hear that Mr. Tucker has decreed that Mr. Boucher is to leave Ottawa.
In 1949 we had the same problem, this time just before a federal election. "Send me down 14 Liberal members," said the Minister of Agriculture and Mr. Tucker, "and everything will be fine." Well, the Liberal members came down, but we still have no dam.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Just the members.

I remember that in 1949 someone sent me a specimen of the election literature of the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McCusker) in which he said, "Send me to Ottawa, if you want water in Regina." Well, Regina still wants water.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: They are building the pipe line now.

My hon. friend reminds me of a bus driver I met in the north of Ireland. I had been travelling for three weeks, almost always in the rain, going east to the Atlantic coast, going across on the boat. For three weeks it rained steadily. I said to the Irish bus driver, "Is it always raining like this? Does the sun never shine?" "Oh," he said, "sir, just give it time." And I presume my hon. friend from Regina will be saying at the next election, "Just give us time and we will get you water, and a lot of other things."

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: You will have it there.

The amazing thing was that when we came back in 1949 the minister was very genial. He had just won and was very pleased. When we said, "Well now, here you are with your Liberal majority; when do we get the dam?" he said, "Well, you cannot do anything without the co-operation of the provinces." Premier Douglas' letter was swift in reply to that.
But still nothing was done. I remember suggestions that the minister had changed his attitude, and he said, "There is no change in attitude. It is our child. Why should we desert it now?" Well, I should go back to my Irish history again. I remember that when certain old ladies went around in the cities wearing their black shawls and begging for money they always borrowed a little child, because it would make a better appeal to the public. It makes me think of the minister whose child, this project, has nevei grown up. It is just the same size yeai after year; and between elections he would like to leave it on the provincial doorstep.
Here we are in 1953, with another electior in the offing. I can say that we, all of us including the minister and the government have come to the end of the road. The min ister told us that he had gone underground Well, that is a very significant phrase. I: he knows anything about English hunting he will know what that phrase means. A better expression would be to say that he hac gone to earth; that is the phrase they use
It has been a long road; I cannot call it i crooked road because that might be unpar
