South Saskatchewan River Project liamentary; but I can say it has been a tortuous one. I suggest the minister is now at the end of it. We have now come to the time when there can be no more deviation. Now is the time of decision.
I note that the minister described the report as a silly dam report; I suggest he could have changed the order of the words and still have been right. I am pleased to note that the minister is still in favour of the project.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is all a matter of how you spell it.

But I would like to remind the minister, when he is thinking in these terms, that a negative decision involves him as the responsible minister of the government, whether he is in favour of it or whether he is not in favour of it personally. And I suggest he had better find out as soon as possible. Since he has never discussed the matter with the cabinet, I suggest now would be a good time to start because, as I have said, he will have to shoulder the responsibility for that decision.
There has been some talk of what was said and was not said away back in 1943. There have been references to what was promised and what was not promised. It all looks very confusing. I ran into an interesting thing which goes back to 1944 or 1945, certainly to a time prior to the 1945 election. Then a Liberal candidate speaking at Moose Jaw before the election of 1945 said:
There is still a lot of detail work to be done-
He can say that again now.
-but the main lines have been thoroughly gone into and it has been found to be economically sound, and will be commenced immediately the men are available to do the work.
At that time there was a shortage of labour. Then there was a paid advertisement in the Moose Jaw Times-Herald, under the sponsorship of the Liberal party of Saskatchewan. This was just before the election, and it read:
The southern Saskatchewan Thunder creek irrigation project alone will undoubtedly contribute much to the prosperity of both our city and surrounding district, which interests are interlocking. This project will be commenced immediately men and material are available.
Finished long ago.

Then on the last sheet there is a quotation from a broadcast, I presume a political one, made by my hon. friend the attorney general of Saskatchewan. This is back in 1944, previous to the 1945 election. What a prophet he was when he said:
I am prepared to go out on a limb and predict that in spite of their definite promises and pledges


the Liberals will advance the scheme just far enough in the next four or five years to use it again as bait in the next federal election. I realize I can be made to look foolish if the prediction turns out wrong but I know the Liberals well enough to be without fear that the limb I am on will break off under me.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: How right he was.

How right he was. One can get a certain amount of humour out of this situation, but I should like to say just a word or two to my hon. friends who live in eastern Canada. Their problem is not caused by not having enough water, but by having too much. You have it all around you in your lakes, rivers and streams. I do not think my hon. friends from the eastern part of Canada can get the picture at all, for instance in regard to dry farming. They are not dry farming conscious; they are not drought conscious.
It is true you had a depression here, but we had to face the effects of that world depression plus the ruination of our farm industry by drought. It was a case of depression plus starvation. In the east you had some industry, there was something going on, and you had food. May I say that food was one thing which some of the people in those areas in Saskatchewan, as my hon. friends well know, just did not have.
In thinking of the national interest, let us consider what was spent on relief in those days. I have not the figure, but I believe it was $187 million.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Altogether, over the period.
$186 million.

I know there were two 10-year periods when the amounts spent were practically the same, and my point is that if those amounts were added together you would have enough to build this South Saskatchewan river dam. It would have been more than enough to build it in those days. That money came out of the pockets of the national taxpayer. These things recur; this may happen again and this dam and irrigation project would be insurance against that particular type of misfortune.
My eastern friends have had no experience with drought. They do not know what it is to live through a dust storm, to see the constantly-sifting sand piling up on the road allowances in great mounds by the telephone poles, mounds which are still there today but fortunately now covered with green grass.
I noticed one silly line in the report where someone said that after all green grass did not bring about a prosperous economy. I want to say to him that the difference between

green and grey is a matter of life and death, the difference between starvation and existence.
Many people in Saskatchewan found that out. Men had to shoot down their stock with the possible exception of one milch cow. A farmer would go to the nearest town to buy a single bale of hay to haul back in his buggy to feed the cow. People in the east have no conception of these things. They have no idea how the Russian thistles piled up against the fences and gates. They do not know how our precious six inches of topsoil, practically our only source of wealth in Saskatchewan, was deposited in the ditches and along the road allowances or at any point where it could be piled up by the wind. That precious topsoil was depleted. Then we had the invasion of grasshoppers which ate the small bit of green grass that had been left.
There was the trek north. Between 1930 and 1937, every morning in Saskatoon we would be awakened at five or six o'clock by the wagons going north. You would look out and see a pitiful hayrack with a team of thin horses, a cook stove, probably a barrel containing most of the household goods, and sometimes a single cow tied behind. There might be three or four children and the mother. They were heading northwest in pursuit of that green grass which the report says is not too important. It was in that way that Loon Lake and Meadow Lake and many other districts were settled by those who are living there today. Since the rains have come many of them have returned to their old homes.
I have tried to tell of these conditions, but the reality was much worse than anything I can describe. We have seen these things and we are conscious of them. Easterners may not believe it, but every Sunday afternoon in the summer three or four hundred cars will drive up to a small dam near my home for one purpose only, just to watch the water go by. Those of us who came through that experience of drought have a realization of what water is worth. That water is going down to the sea, yet it could mean life to parched land, it is water which would provide a livelihood for farmers, increased prosperity for our towns and added industry. In the name of my' own city and the constituency of Saskatoon I ask that this project be proceeded with forthwith.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment which was placed before the house on the motion to go into supply presents an opportunity for hon. members to express their opinion as to whether there should or should
South Saskatchewan River Project not be definite provision by the government for the construction of a dam on the South Saskatchewan river along with the other works that would go with it.
This afternoon the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) gave his reasons for not supporting the amendment to the motion to go into supply, and also for not supporting the subamendment.
He says the statement in the amendment which has been moved is not correct. He indicates that there is a provision in the estimates for a sum of money, and for that reason he cannot support the amendment. He has made it abundantly clear in his statement to the house this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, that the figure included in the estimates is not for construction. Let that be clearly in the mind of every hon. member who seeks an excuse in the statement of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) this afternoon for voting against the amendment before the house.

In order to keep the record
straight, may I call attention to the fact that at page 121 of the estimates there are four items:	Bow river irrigation project, St.
Mary irrigation project, South Saskatchewan river development, and Buffalo Pound lake reservoir, and the others all include construction. They are all under construction, and there is no reason why this amount cannot be used in the same way.

The minister has made it
abundantly clear this afternoon that this is not for construction. In fact all his earlier statements would have been meaningless if it were for construction, because he told us this afternoon that he has never at any time said that this construction was going ahead. I must confess that came as a surprise after some of the reports that have appeared from time to time in the press. Nevertheless that is his statement. If that is his statement, then it would seem quite obvious that the item included in the estimates is not for construction. Since it is not for construction then it is appropriate that those members who think there should be construction should have the opportunity to express their opinion in the manner provided by the amendment and the subamendment.
The reason the minister has given for not supporting the subamendment is that the P.F.R.A. engineers have not made recommendations. Some members will have difficulty in determining when a recommendation becomes a recommendation if the statement of the minister is correct. Most certainly the engineers who have served with the P.F.R.A.

South Saskatchewan River Project administration have been very emphatic in publicly making their recommendation on different occasions that this project should be proceeded with. The report on the South Saskatchewan river project, printed by the king's printer with the heading "Department of Agriculture" and carrying the date of April, 1951, gives a long series of benefits which the engineers say would result from proceeding with this development. They put forward the benefits that would result from irrigation, power, municipal water supply and recreation.
Not only have they given their explanation of the extensive benefits that would result from the development, but in public they have indicated quite clearly their belief that it should be proceeded with. The minister this afternoon has made it rather difficult for us to understand exactly what his position is. He has told us that never at any time has he made the statement that the South Saskatchewan river dam was going to be built. Undoubtedly that will be disappointing to many people who thought he had. Undoubtedly they will expect some further explanation of the reports, which he would now appear to regard as erroneous, giving the very opposite impression. The words he used were:	"On no occasion at any time
have I stated that the South Saskatchewan river dam was going to be built." Those words make it clear that there should be a motion before the house to give some of us a chance to say by a vote, which is the only way we can say it effectively, that this dam should be built and that the project should be proceeded with.
There is one thing in regard to which I think there will be agreement on both sides of the house. The minister has said that this is not a subject of concern only to the people of Saskatchewan. With that I am sure there will be general agreement. The subject is one of interest to every Canadian who believes that we are citizens of one country, and that it is the responsibility of the members of this house, from whatever part of Canada they come and on whichever side of the house they sit, to bear in mind that our responsibility is to the people of Canada as a people living in one country which we all serve.
The Minister of Agriculture left us in some uncertainty as to what his exact meaning was. In spite of some interesting revelations as to discussions in cabinet council, he has told us that this subject has never been discussed by the government of Canada in council. He left some uncertainty as to that positive statement by his reference to


the various occasions when items have been entered in the estimates for the necessary preliminary work. Nevertheless, as the Speaker has pointed out on different occasions, we are bound to accept the statement of the minister; and his statement is that this subject has never yet been discussed by the government of Canada in council.
That is the question as to whether we are going to build the dam.

That is what X understood. The minister has now again confirmed the fact that never yet in cabinet council has the question been discussed of whether or not they would proceed with the dam. On the basis of that statement I submit there is every reason why we should be considering an amendment such as we have before us and why hon. members should indicate to the government by their votes that they do want this project proceeded with.
There may be some suggestion that the facts are not yet available. There may be some suggestion that a further inquiry should be conducted. Surely there must be some end to inquiries before action is taken. Of course I do agree that this government has established the practice of conducting inquiries into inquiries, and apparently it is a habit that is catching. But in this particular case there have been so many inquiries, the subject has been under consideration for so long, that one would have thought that by this time the government would be in a position to hear some discussion of this subject. No matter what the outcome of the vote on the amendment may be, I strongly urge the Minister of Agriculture that for the first time he give the cabinet the benefit of his knowledge of this subject, because I think they might be interested in the South Saskatchewan dam and also in whether or not this subject, which is discussed so much in Saskatchewan, might not also be discussed by the cabinet which is the executive body of parliament.
I for one am greatly surprised to hear for the first time this afternoon that it has never been discussed although we have discussed it so frequently in the house. That very fact of course naturally fortifies the opinion of those of us who think that 4t should be discussed and that it would be helpful for the government to hear views expressed on it, since they have not received the benefit of the views of the minister in cabinet council.
This subject has been under consideration in different ways for a very long time. In fact it was first discussed before confederation, before 1867. It had been pointed out

that it would be highly desirable to augment the waters of the South Saskatchewan river by the construction of a dam at an appropriate place. Throughout long years the possibility of using water power in that river has been under consideration. It is now considerably more than forty years since I visited that river for the first time and was told by people living in that area of the wonderful results that would flow from the construction of a dam, and the use of water for irrigation and power. It has been under consideration for a very long time.
During the years since people were convinced that this would be a desirable project hundreds of millions of dollars worth of unused energy has flowed down that river because the decision has not been made. Throughout all these years whatever water power was there in potential form has gone to waste. Throughout all these years whatever water could have been used for irrigation has also been unused.
Granted that there must always be some time of beginning, granted that the reasons for proceeding with this development were not so apparent in those early years as they are today, the fact remains that throughout the last twenty years at least there has been the most convincing evidence of the necessity for the effective use of the water resources that are available in that area, and for the development also of whatever power potential can be harnessed on the South Saskatchewan.
This subject must be of interest to all members of this house who are called upon to consider other ventures at the same time. To many of us it must seem strange that it is only in the case of this particular development that it seems to be so necessary to refer the responsibility to a royal commission. There was no royal commission appointed when it was decided to support the Canadian Pacific Railway which gave us transportation right across Canada. Engineers were employed by the government and upon the advice of those engineers the government acted. At that time the government was not told that there was no population adequate to use the rail services that would cross the prairies. At that time the government acted in the belief that the way to get population there was to provide that facility.
There was no royal commission appointed at the time it was decided by another Conservative government years later to create the Canadian National Railways by the amalgamation of different services across the
South Saskatchewan River Project country. They acted on the advice of engineers, and the decision was made upon the advice of competent engineers at that time.
There was no royal commission appointed to find out whether it was appropriate for the taxpayers of Canada to construct a canal across the Niagara peninsula. Competent engineers were employed and their decisions and recommendations guided the government at that time. There was no royal commission appointed to inquire into the construction and the subsequent expansion and development of the Sault canals, and the power made available from that source. There again competent engineers were relied upon and the decisions taken on their recommendations.
This house has on different occasions been called upon to indicate its views in regard to the St. Lawrence deep waterway, something that will undoubtedly be of benefit to a particular part of Canada. Nevertheless it is to be regarded with satisfaction on the part of Canadians generally that no local consideration has guided the expressions of members of this house in their discussions of this subject. With admirable recognition of the unity of Canada in matters of this kind, members of this house from right across Canada have indicated their belief that although the development of this St. Lawrence deep waterway will undoubtedly most greatly benefit Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba-and undoubtedly Ontario most of all-it is something that meets with the approval of all members because of the increased economic strength that will come to Canada and the increased production which will result from this development.
I submit that hon. members of this house, on both sides of the house, should regard this matter in the same light and should be prepared to accord the same measure of support to this project in Saskatchewan that they have accorded to the St. Lawrence deep waterway and to these other projects which have all been regarded as part of the expanding development of a great nation. It is in that light that we should express our opinions here.
I was interested in the statement by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McCusker) that he would like to support this idea but that the motion, in his opinion, constituted a want of confidence motion and, therefore, he would be unable to support it. One might ask when the members on the opposite side would ever be free to support any such motion. In fact, although I must be very cautious not to suggest any lack of independence in their thinking, one might almost

South Saskatchewan River Project wonder just how that independence is to be expressed if they are to be unable to support any recommendation that has not been put before this house by the government itself. Certainly I would think some of them would welcome the opportunity to assert that independence which has been proclaimed so vigorously in this house by supporting a project of this nature, particularly when it has been stated by the hon. member who moved it that he is quite prepared that this should not be regarded as a want of confidence motion, but rather that he wants this considered as a motion that will permit a free expression of the members of this house that we want this important development in Saskatchewan to proceed as part of the development of Canada as a whole.
That course has been followed on other occasions. There have been occasions when ministers of the crown directly concerned with the subject matter of resolutions have said:	We ask that this be regarded as a
free vote.
I would ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), as the minister primarily responsible in this case, to inform the house that he asks that the vote be a free vote; and that although the government have not discussed this subject, nevertheless they have permitted him to indicate that this motion will not be regarded as a want of confidence motion. That would be very helpful to those who, like the hon. member for Regina, would wish to vote for it but feel restrained because, although they are completely independent, they nevertheless feel concerned about the fact that the vote might be misinterpreted if, by any chance, enough of them voted for the amendment to actually carry it on this occasion.
It would be a very healthy thing, Mr. Speaker, and it would bring fresh confidence to the people of Canada in the real independence of thought in this if, first of all, we had a statement by the right hon. Minister of Agriculture that this is a free vote; and then if we had an indication by the members that they are sufficiently free to support an amendment which has as its purpose the declaration of our common interest in Saskatchewan as well as every other part of Canada. Even if the Minister of Agriculture hesitates to give this assurance in view of the fact that he has not discussed the subject with the cabinet, nevertheless I would hope there would be some hon. members from Saskatchewan and other parts of Canada as well who would say-

If I may be permitted a
correction, I have not moved anything in the 

house at all. It is not my motion that is before the house, and it is not my amendment that is before the house.
Just your baby.

The right hon. Minister of
Agriculture surely can be forgiven for thinking that it might be his motion because he has spoken about the subject so often; and because he has spoken about the subject so often, one would have thought he would have welcomed the opportunity to ask for the free support of a motion which interprets the view he has expressed over and over again in this house and outside of it.
This is not his motion, but I am suggesting that it is a motion that is entirely consistent with the view he has expressed, and that if he will only ask the government to listen to him for the first time in regard to this subject and then, after they have heard him, to give him the authority to call for a free vote, then with that encouragement we might actually get from the members of this house an expression of opinion in support of something that I believe the majority of the members of this house want and would like to vote for if they did not find, for one reason or another, that they were not prepared to declare their opinion at this time.
It will be a nice way to send a message to the government.

Since the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has never carried this subject to the cabinet, it would be helpful if someone else did so; and this is one chance we will all get. I would hope that some of the hon. members will look at the situation in that light.
I have not said that I have not carried the subject to the cabinet. I said that the subject has not been discussed by the cabinet.
Am I to take it that the minister carried it to the cabinet and that they refused to discuss a subject which he brought there?
No.

I am discussing this matter in all seriousness. What the Minister of Agriculture has now said is that he did not say that it had not been carried to the cabinet. He only says that they have not discussed it. If those words mean anything at all, they mean that he carried it to the government and they would not listen to him. We have the chance to ask the government to listen to him on this occasion.
It has not been discussed.

The minister again repeats that it has not been discussed. Since he indicates that he has carried it to the government and that it has not been discussed, may I repeat that this is a chance for hon. members, by their vote, to carry this subject to the government and to help the minister to get this subject before the government in spite of their earlier refusal to listen to him.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, that is carrying the matter a little bit beyond what most of us would find easy to accept. Of course we must and do accept the minister's statement that it has not been discussed. But we thought the minister was one who usually insisted upon being heard. I think most of us will regret to learn that a minister who is so vigorous in his statements in this house is so unsuccessful in making himself heard in cabinet council.
I will be heard at the right time.
You will be heard yet.

I did not say that.

That was the statement to which I was referring in the remarks that I have just made.
This of course is not by any manner of means the first time this matter has been under consideration. The minister has read from an editorial in the Calgary Albertan. I therefore feel sure that he will not object to my referring to an editorial in the Regina Leader-Post which appeared on February 4 under the heading "Can't Swap Horses in Midstream."

speechtext: Horses again?
Horses again.
I hope the minister will not think that in this there is any suggestion other than the ordinary colloquial reference to the word "horse" in a statement of this kind.
They did not change any horses for ducks, anyway.
They are not on the payroll there yet.
It won't be long now.

No; the horses referred to in this editorial are not on the payroll. This editorial has this to say. In view of the minister's reference to the other editorial, I think it might be well to put this on the record:
The Hogg commission is not the first one to investigate irrigation. In 1941, in order to obtain guidance for its rehabilitation program, the federal government established the Meek commission.
It studied the St. Mary-Milk river project, and declared in its report the following year:
"It has become a generally accepted principle that the total costs of an irrigation project of this magnitude should not be charged to the lands immediately benefited. To insure completion and successful operation of the project there must be governmental assistance. The development of the St. Mary and Milk rivers project would not only be of benefit locally and provincially but would we believe be to the general advantage of Canada."
The Meek commission recommended that the federal government pay the costs of water storage as a non-recoverable contribution to the project. This subsequently became government policy with the passage of an order in council in 1947.
The Hogg commission virtually brushed aside this finding of the Meek commission. It loaded all the irrigation and most of the water storage costs on the land and on the basis of the outlandish $250 million cost estimate declared each irrigation farm 
would represent an investment of $70,000. This was one of the grounds on which it rejected the project "for the present."
Which was right, the Hogg commission or the Meek commission? Experience in every country where irrigation has been adopted on a large scale proves beyond doubt that the Meek commission was correct in declaring that the land alone cannot carry the full burden of costs. In fact, in the United States it is contended that the national benefits from irrigation are sufficiently great to justify the state paying 85 per cent of the costs- a much greater percentage than is envisaged under federal policy based on the Meek findings.
If the federal government swaps horses in midstream, while its rehabilitation job in the west is only partially completed, by belatedly rejecting the Meek report and refashioning its policy on the Hogg report, it will be dealing most unfairly with Saskatchewan.
Without quoting the remainder of that editorial, I would simply point out that it does go on to urge that the government proceed with this project which has been so long under discussion.
The commission report on the South Saskatchewan river, which was presented to this house, makes a number of recommendations which are to be found on pages 6, 7 and 8, and which must be extremely hard for anyone to accept who has followed the course of these inquiries over the years by the engineers of the P.F.R.A., by the Meek commission and by others who have inquired into this subject.
The first recommendation deals with the question of the economic returns and says that they are not commensurate at present with the cost of the project, although the project would yield social returns which "while they cannot be measured for the purpose of this report, would be of great value to the region in which it is situated."
The second recommendation says that when the time comes that this project should be proceeded with, those who are making the decision should take these matters into account:
(a)	The prospect of adequate markets for the specialty crops such as sugar beets, canning vegetables, potatoes, etc., that would be grown on the area it is proposed to irrigate.
(b)	The Canadian demand for farm products
which, when it comes more nearly into balance with production, would require a more intensive use of land resources;	.
(c)	A significant change in relationship of the price of farm products and construction costs;
(d)	The necessity for the construction of public works for the relief of unemployment.
These are things that are to be considered before this is to be proceeded with. If the government had waited for population on the prairies before it built the Canadian Pacific Railway there would not be a railway across

Canada yet. If the great hydroelectric development in Ontario had waited for customers, there would not be the largest publicly-owned project of this kind in the world today in that province. If in the case of railways built through the north lands of this country for development purposes they had waited for population, there would not yet be any population or any development in those areas.
In this country of ours, with all the immense opportunities that lie ahead, it is our duty to visualize what can come from developments of this kind and not expect the population to get there ahead of the project which is essential for their occupation of that land. If there is going to be population in this central Palliser triangle, then those people must be assured that they are going to have irrigation and power for the purposes of their daily lives in that area. The project must be assured. It must be proceeded with before the population will get there. The government certainly is putting the cart before the horse if it accepts those recommendations as the basis of the timing of this development.
The third recommendation of the commission was:
The commission finds that the available data, which are by no means complete, indicate that the said project does not represent the most profitable and desirable use which can be made of the physical resources involved.
Why is the information not complete? If the information is not complete, why have we the report? Surely it is a subject that could be considered by competent engineers.
The fourth recommendation is:
The commission recommends, in respect to No. 3 above, that further study be given to the merits of:
(a) Irrigating the area that needs water most;
(b) Bringing additional land under irrigation in the Saskatchewan river basin by pumping water direct from the river and from existing irrigation canals or extensions thereof:
(c)	The development known as the Red Deer river project, including its possible extension into the province of Saskatchewan.
The fifth recommendation is:
The commission finds that the future demand for water for irrigation could be such as to exhaust the available flow of the South Saskatchewan river, and recommends, therefore, that without delay a comprehensive, long-range program be developed that would result, over the years, in the most beneficial use being made in the interests of the people of Canada of the waters of the Saskatchewan river from its head waters to the sea.
The sixth recommendation is:
The commission finds that to implement a basin program, the conflict between the upstream consumptive use of the water for irrigation and its downstream use for generating power will have to be resolved.

After all this inquiry and all these recommendations we have boxed the compass and we are back exactly to where we started. This commission, set up and carried forward at considerable expense to the people of Canada, recommends that the government make inquiries in consultation with the provinces, and presumably act on those inquiries.
That has all been done, as I said this afternoon.

the minister misapprehends the recommendation. This recommendation is referring to the South Saskatchewan dam.

Not only have we the set-up, as the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) knows. got to see the record.

They could have seen it; I
do not know whether they did or not.

The report is very clearly written. In the eighth recommendation the commission recommends certain consideration

South Saskatchewan River Project in regard to other developments which are set out. Then there is a ninth recommendation and a tenth recommendation which relate to subjects the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) felt, I gather, were really outside the scope of the original matter; and that, I believe, is in accordance with the opinion of many hon. members.
One of the difficulties one faces in connection with this matter is that on the one hand the minister says, "We have done all these things" and on the other hand he says that this has not been discussed with the government.

No, not those things. Those matters have all been discussed with the government and passed upon, and they are part of government policy. The matter of the building of the dam has not been discussed by the government.
Oh, that is it.

They are interested.

Well, the reference to this commission was to inquire into the South Saskatchewan river project. The recommendations to which I have been referring are the recommendations of that commission, which had those instructions; and we now have their recommendations before us.
The commission also makes it clear that there are considerable social advantages connected with the plan. Anyone who has visited the area must know the extent of those advantages. He would know about the abandoned homes and the abandoned school houses in the area. He would know also about the experimental developments that have taken place, and of the demonstration near Outlook which is there for anyone to see, which shows what can be done if that soil is properly irrigated. The minister referred to that, in fact, this afternoon. There is no question but that the soil is rich and fertile, if irrigation can be carried to it.
This commission report does not find that the water cannot be carried there. It does present difficulties. It indicates certain considerations that should be kept in mind. Undoubtedly those considerations should be kept in mind by the engineers of the government. But this report does confirm that the dam can be built at the Coteau creek site. It does confirm that the water is available for purposes of power and irrigation. It does confirm that it is a practical engineering project.


The objections are based very considerably upon the estimated cost, more than twice the amount of the estimates set out in the engineering findings under P.F.R.A. who, basing their findings on 1950 costs, estimated that the whole project would cost about $103,700,000. That would be divided between the dominion and provincial governments. The government of Saskatchewan has stated publicly that it is prepared to accept its share of the cost.
When the evidence is clear that this heartland of Saskatchewan can be improved in this way; when the evidence is clear that an area which has suffered so greatly from drought and the social consequences of drought can be returned to a productive condition; when the evidence is clear that the soil can become perhaps more arable than it has ever been before; and when the reports before us demonstrate that profitable crops can be raised in the area if irrigation and power were made available at the site, then I submit that with the findings of the competent engineers of P.F.R.A. and the findings of other engineers available to us, and with the recommendation of the engineers employed by the government on other occasions, it is appropriate that the members of this House of Commons give a clear declaration of their belief that the government should now say that this project will be proceeded with and that the irrigation and electrical developments will be undertaken so they may bring a new vitality, a new prosperity, a new hope and new population to the people living in that central part of the great Palliser triangle.
Not only are there social and economic consequences, but there is also to be considered the very direct effect this will have upon the people of Saskatchewan generally. It is only natural that people who have been encouraged for so long to believe that this project was going to be undertaken are now discouraged and disheartened by the apparent acceptance of the negative findings of this commission, which was set up with the knowledge that those who were being appointed were predisposed against this dam project.
This project is vital to the heart of Saskatchewan. This project is sound from the engineering point of view; it is sound from the social point of view; it is sound from the national point of view. The only question that could be asked is this:	Is it economically sound? The P.F.R.A. engineers and other engineers report that it is. Without making adequate inquiry themselves, the recent commission have given figures which

are so highly inflated as to be discredited by anyone who has had earlier contact with the subject.
Let us remember that with the unanimous support of hon. members of the House of Commons steps have been taken from time to time to meet situations arising from unsatisfactory conditions in that area. As the minister has pointed out, the area has suffered great hardship. The government has been called upon to spend money to assist the people there. It would be far better if the money were spent on the productive enterprise that is now before us. The amendment before hon. members gives them an opportunity to support an expression of that kind. I would hope that, first of all, after due consideration the minister would inform members of the house, as ministers have on other occasions, that as has been suggested by the opposition, they are free to vote in support of the motion without its being regarded as a want of confidence vote. Then, with that freedom to vote as they wish I would hope that hon. members from every part of Canada, from Newfoundland to British Columbia, would say by their vote: As part of a great national reclamation and conservation project, we want this development proceeded with right away.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend tonight to take up much of the time of the house in participating in this debate. At the outset I should like to say that my conscience is quite clear in voting against the amendment and the subamendment now before the house. When we come to the estimates of the Department of Agriculture and deal with the item having to do with the South Saskatchewan project, I shall support that item.
I have noticed during the debate that hon. members have gone back many years in the course of their speeches. Some went back to the days of confederation in 1867, some went back to 1916, some referred to the thirties. I could say considerable about the thirties, but I think that period has been pretty well covered. I think the people of Canada are fairly familiar with what happened in the western provinces during the thirties, so I shall refrain from going into that again.
South Saskatchewan River Project
Tonight I intend to go back only to 1951, and for this reason. On July 15, 1951, I started out by motor from my farm. I headed south on No. 4 highway and passed through the towns of Biggar and Rosetown. Finally we reached Swift Current, where we turned to journey west on No. 1 highway. That evening we stopped at the town of Taber in the province of Alberta. I mention this because on arriving there I had my first opportunity of seeing just what irrigation could do. I understand that at that time, because of the rainfall they had been having, it had not been found necessary to use the facilities available, but I could see the facilities that were there if required. I saw sugar beets growing and some splendid grain crops. Unfortunately, about two hours before we arrived in Taber a streak of hail had gone through that country and we saw the effect on those beautiful crops.
The following morning we arrived in Lethbridge where we found great commotion because that afternoon the St. Mary river dam was to be officially opened. Lethbridge was buzzing with people and cars. After lunch I journeyed with many thousands of people down to the site of the dam some 40 miles south of Lethbridge, and had a chance to have a good look at the project.
The official opening was under the chairmanship of our great roving reporter, Mr. John Fisher. The proceedings got under way and, if I remember correctly, the first speech we heard as we looked out toward the Rocky mountains was by the master of ceremonies, Mr. Fisher. He was followed by the premier of Alberta. Then at the appropriate moment the one who was to officially open the dam came into the picture. I should like to quote the words of the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) at the time he officially opened that dam. When he put his hands on the lever in the control tower of the irrigation works and released the water from the reservoir into the main canal on its way to the land in the area, he said:
It gives me great pleasure to turn the waters, from the first nationally-constructed large reservoir, upon the fertile lands of southern Alberta. I consider the inauguration of this policy as the outstanding and most helpful achievement of my period as Minister of Agriculture for Canada over fifteen years. I trust it is only the beginning of a development which will multiply Canadian homes in the west.
The next day it was my privilege to sit in at the annual meeting of the western Canada reclamation association being held in Lethbridge. In the afternoon I was called upon by the chairman to say a few words, and I should like to repeat a few of the things I said on that occasion. One thing

South Saskatchewan River Project was quite conspicuous at that meeting; that was the absence of any representatives of one of the western provinces.
I said on that occasion, and I repeat it tonight, that we as members of parliament, when discussing these large projects, should try to look at them and consider them on a high plane. We should look at them from the broad national viewpoint instead of a narrow provincial viewpoint.
On our way back we were discussing the South Saskatchewan project. I think that project should be proceeded with for two reasons. If proceeded with it would create a lake 140 miles long in the centre of the Palliser triangle and would irrigate some 125,000 or 130,000 acres by gravity alone. I think those two reasons are sufficient, as far as I am concerned, for making a start on this project. I should like to read a short passage from the report, and I quote from page 10 as follows:
The Importance of the Prairies to Canada's Economy
7. The commercial attributes of agricultural expansion in western Canada have been defined with great lucidity by Professor Fowke in his historical review of the economic development of the prairie provinces, prepared for the commission. (Part II, chapter 3)
Western agricultural expansion, (he wrote), led to eastern urbanization, to the growth and prosperity of commercial and industrial centres. To equip and service the agricultural frontier there was necessarily a tremendous increase in the manufacturing, merchandising and transportation facilities of the country. The frontier farmer is typically a trader. He sells much and buys more, financing the difference by the accumulation of debt. Westward over the continental trade routes, over rivers and increasingly over railways, there moved the manufactured products of eastern cities. Eastward in return there moved the products of the expanding agricultural areas, cereals, livestock and livestock products. The national income and the national revenues multiplied, partly as a direct result of increased agricultural production but more particularly because of the commercial and industrial employments which followed inevitably in the wake of agricultural immigration and settlement.
I mentioned that we should try to keep this on a high plane, and that is just what I intend to do myself. However, I arr rather concerned about some of the alterna ve schemes that may be mentioned. Mentii .n has been made of the North Saskatchewan river. It has been brought into the picture of the South Saskatchewan dam. It is quite noticeable that there are two cities in the southern part of Saskatchewan that are not situated on the banks of a river, and they are having, and have had for a long period of time, a great water shortage. I refer to the cities of Regina and Moose Jaw. On the North Saskatchewan river there are three cities that
are developing at a great pace at the present time, the cities of Edmonton, North Battleford and Prince Albert.
So far as bringing water from the North Saskatchewan down to the South Saskatchewan is concerned, may I suggest that this might be a case of robbing Peter to pay Paul. I can tell hon. members from actual experience and knowledge that the provincial department of highways has had great trouble in operating ferries across the North Saskatchewan river during the past five or ten years. Many ferries have been abandoned for no other reason than that during many weeks in the summer and fall there is not sufficient water for them to ply back and forth across the river. They are flat-bottomed ferries, but even so many of them have had to be removed from service and abandoned.
That is one of the reasons the people of the Lloydminster district and in the area across the river north of Lloydminster, where rail facilities are sorely needed, are in dire need of a bridge on the meridian line immediately north of Lloydminster. The fact is that on many occasions when you go down to the ferry you will see a sign as you approach reading "No crossing", and you take it for granted that the water is low.
I know there are others who intend to speak in this debate, but there is one other point I should like to mention. It is suggested that the pumping of water for irrigation would be a cost against the project. Water now being wasted would be used to generate electricity for pumping, so it could not be counted a cost. Is the commission's ratio of values fair, based as it is on land values and commodity prices of the past against costs of construction of today? May I suggest that the ratio has remained the same for the reason that as costs have advanced so have commodity prices and land values.
In conclusion, while many figures have been quoted in the report of the commission and by others with respect to the South Saskatchewan project, I understand that figures submitted by engineers and others engaged in the construction of such projects indicate that the estimated cost of the construction of the dam, which is the federal government's responsibility, would be in the neighbourhood of $68 to $84 million. In view of these figures-and even suppose the cost should reach $100 million-I would say that if money can be made available for the St. Lawrence seaway then money can be made available for this project, because both will be beneficial to the Canadian economy. We have the tools. Let us get on with the job.

Mr. Speaker, this debate may well be more important than many hon. members realize. If the results of the next election are close, the Saskatchewan constituencies which are affected by this project may decide whether the government wins or loses. In my opinion the speech of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) this afternoon was disappointing. One fact did seem to emerge, that for this session at least the South Saskatchewan river project is a dead issue.
During the debate so far I have been rather surprised at the attitude of my friends from Saskatchewan who are members of the Liberal party. One member after another, including the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Bater), who has just spoken, the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McCusker) and others, has stated that he favours building this dam. If that is so, I cannot understand why they are not prepared to let their votes follow their voices.
The amendment moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) is very clear. It reads as follows:
This house regrets that in the estimates presented to this house no provision has been made for immediately proceeding with the construction of the South Saskatchewan river dam.
No one can take objection to that amendment. It is a simple one, and I challenge members of the Liberal party from my home province to vote as their consciences tell them. On this issue members from Saskatchewan should be just as unanimous as are the people of Saskatchewan. I do not think this is the time for technicalities. I do not think this is the time for fence sitting. Therefore when the vote does come, I appeal to them to support the amendment.
This afternoon the Minister of Agriculture made the rather amazing statement that the cabinet had not yet discussed this issue. If that is so, I respectfully suggest that he bring it before them immediately. If they are not prepared to take a sympathetic viewpoint, then I suggest that he should join the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) and resign from the cabinet.
I should like to say a few words to eastern and maritime members. I was pleased to notice this afternoon that a Toronto member, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees), supported this project as did the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew). It is a project which is national in character. I am afraid that some hon. members like the hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Gauthier) have an idea that the project is just another handout for Saskatchewan. I think that is what he termed it at dinner time today.
South Saskatchewan River Project
It is anything but another handout. It is not a government expense. This project is a capital investment, and it is self-liquidating. Over the years it will save this country millions of dollars in relief costs. It will result in the production of millions of dollars worth of additional crops and a great deal of revenue from hydro power. Therefore I appeal to hon. members from other parts of the country to recognize that it is a national project. As has been pointed out, we from Saskatchewan have supported such projects for the maritimes as the Canso causeway and dikes for New Brunswick. In central Canada we have supported the St. Lawrence seaway, in Alberta several dam projects, and so on. Today we are asking for the same kind of consideration for Saskatchewan.
It is quite true that in recent years our province has been relatively prosperous. It is quite true that moisture conditions have been good, but the house must be aware of the fact that another drought can come at any time. As a matter of fact we have had so many good years that, if we can judge from history, another dry period could arrive in 1953. I lived through the last such period and I can say that for several years there was not a blade of grass in the whole province. I saw crops wither and die. I saw thousands of cattle slaughtered or moved out of the province. Dust storms in those days were so severe you could not see across the street. I recall driving a car on many occasions and hardly being able to see the end of the engine for dust. I remember that my home city of Moose Jaw had the water turned off twelve hours a day for about six months in order to conserve water supplies. Our local packing plant had to close down because it could not get water. In the year 1937 about one-half of all the people in Saskatchewan were receiving government aid of one kind or another.
These were the conditions not very many years ago. As a matter of fact you can still find empty houses, schools and ghost towns which are a kind of memorial to the exodus of the people who lived in those areas.
Citizens of Saskatchewan fear that another such period may come along. We do not think that is necessary, because one of the mightiest of all Canadian rivers flows unused right through the heart of the dust bowl and on to Hudson bay. If the government would proceed with this dam the economy of the province could be transformed.
I remind hon. members that many of the so-called backward countries, Spain, India, China and Egypt, have already embarked on far larger projects than the one contemplated on the South Saskatchewan river. Surely

South Saskatchewan River Project then a modern nation like Canada can afford to water our burning plains. I remind hon. members too that since I have come to Ottawa I have seen parliament vote millions and millions of dollars to Britain, Belgium, Ceylon, Holland, Pakistan and other countries. I supported those gifts and I think they were needed; but if our country and this parliament can be so generous to other nations surely it can be equally generous with such a much needed project here at home.
I think the Hogg commission found no major weaknesses in this South Saskatchewan proposal. It did contend that the returns would not be commensurate with the cost. It contended that this dam would cost about $250 million; but the P.F.R.A. a year ago estimated that it would cost only $105 million. For myself, I prefer to take the P.F.R.A. figure. I would point out that the commission used cost figures which were prepared by a Calgary contractor who based his data on the findings of a United States firm called the Morrison-Knudsen Company. According to Engineering News Records of last January, this is the same company which recently submitted a bid of $7 million on a South Dakota project. The Morrison-Knudsen Company bid there was the highest of twelve competitive bids, almost twice the $3 [DOT] 7 million of the successful tenderer. If the company is as wrong on this project as it was on the South Dakota one, I think the P.F.R.A. figure is likely to be a lot closer.
Water is so valuable on the prairies that we cannot afford to let it go to waste any longer. I would join with other hon. members in urging the government at this time to override the recommendations of the commission and start building the dam this year.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to say a few words on the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) and also to speak to the speech made this afternoon by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner).
I am sure we in the house are glad that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is present, because the Minister of Agriculture told us this afternoon that this question which has been before the people of Saskatchewan and western Canada for many years, and the report that has been made by the royal commission, have not yet been brought to the attention of the cabinet. I feel-
I did not go that far.
I beg your pardon?
I did not say that it had not been brought to the attention of the government. I said it was not discussed-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

The Minister of Agriculture is spending the evening trying to get himself out of his loose talk.
I am spending the evening trying to straighten out my hon. friend from Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker).

Have you been changing
Hansard too?
I haven't changed a word. It is just the same as I said it this afternoon, but it is not as my friend from Lake Centre says it is.

You are not asking questions, you are making a statement.

I asked some questions this afternoon and I received some information which I very much appreciate; and I know that the people of Saskatchewan will appreciate it when they learn of the answers. This afternoon the minister made the statement-and if he says he did not he can explain it afterwards-that this report had as yet not been brought to the attention of the government.
He did not say anything of the kind.
Here is a mind reader. He was not here this afternoon.
I was here.
He was not.
I was here all afternoon.

Yes, he was.
Now, Mr. Speaker,-

Mr. Speaker-

It is particularly within my knowledge, having taken down a record of the cabinet ministers who were here.
There was not one cabinet minister here at one time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Citation 240, page 103, Beauchesne's third edition, reads:
It has been formally ruled by Speakers in the Canadian commons that a statement by an hon. member respecting himself and peculiarly within his own knowledge must be accepted, . . .

Mr. Speaker, all I can say in view of your ruling is that I was present here-

Mr. Speaker,-
On a point of order-

Mr. Speaker, on my word of honour I was here during all of the time the Minister of Agriculture spoke; here in the chamber.
It must have been done with mirrors.
There is no question about that, Mr. Speaker. But at the time the questions were asked of the Minister of Agriculture-and that is the time to which I made reference-
The Minister of National Revenue was not here.
I was here; and you won't say that outside.

A great big prize fighter. Well. well.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I do not think hon. members should present the picture that is now being presented in this house.
It should be on television.

I rise to a point of order. Your Honour, I concede, is perfectly correct when you say that an hon. member must accept the statement made by another hon. member as to facts within the knowledge of that hon. member. But I submit, Mr. Speaker, that you are going beyond what is contained in that rule when you say that an hon. member cannot suggest that the facts with reference to which the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) made his statement were not the facts which were in the mind of the hon.

South Saskatchewan River Project member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he made his statement that the minister was not here. Therefore if Your Honour refuses to allow the hon. member for Lake Centre to state the occasion to which he was referring you are, I submit, doing a great injustice to the hon. member who first spoke, and are going far beyond the rule to which Your Honour has referred.
To anyone listening to his speech, it appears that the hon. member for Lake Centre has made statements with reference to the presence of the Minister of National Revenue at a time when certain questions were directed to the Minister of Agriculture. It also appears obvious that the Minister of National Revenue has made a statement with respect to another occasion.
Not at all.

I submit that it is perfectly within the rights of the hon. member for Lake Centre to make clear the occasion to which he was referring and to continue discussion of that matter in an orderly fashion.
You are all mixed up.
If Your Honour refuses to allow the hon. member for Lake Centre to further refer to the matter at all, then I submit that it is an application of the rules which is not apt under the circumstances.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am quite prepared to listen to the hon. member for Lake Centre -I thought that was what I had done-if he wants to say exactly to what speech of the Minister of Agriculture he is referring, whether it is the speech that was made this afternoon. Apparently that is the one we are concerned about. If the hon. member for Lake Centre is referring to a speech made by the Minister of Agriculture a few days ago it may be a different proposition.
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If the reference is to the one made this afternoon, and if the Minister of National Revenue says he was here, it seems to me that the hon. member for Lake Centre must accept the statement.
In reply to an implication which I rather gathered was contained in the remarks made by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), may I say that there is nothing at issue as to the references which the hon. member for Lake Centre might make to the understanding of the Minister of National Revenue of the answer of the Minister of Agriculture. He can talk about that. He can criticize the interpretation, or question whether the Minister of National Revenue heard correctly. He can contradict that. But TMr. Fulton.]

what he cannot contradict or what he must accept is the statement made by the Minister of National Revenue that he was here during the time the Minister of Agriculture spoke this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, there is no reason at all for us to be in disagreement about this matter. The Minister of National Revenue says he was in the house when the Minister of Agriculture was making his speech-
That is right.

-and I have no argument about that. What I am talking about is the occasion when the questioning took place with regard to the Minister of Agriculture, and when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) was speaking, in the course of which the minister was not in his seat in the house.
The hon. member did not say that.
Wait a minute.
The hon. member said I was not in the house.
Let us clear the matter up. Will the minister state where he was?

I said I was in the chamber all the time during which the Minister of Agriculture was speaking, that I spent my afternoon in the house. I was here when he started and when he finished; and on one occasion I was behind the curtain. A gentleman wanted to see me. I was here during all of his speech.
Mr. Speaker, does that not indicate exactly the foundation for the statement I made?
Not at all.
I have not television and I cannot see my hon. friend when he is behind the curtain while at the same time saying that he is in the house. That is exactly the point.
The hon. member backs out gracefully.
There is no disagreement; go ahead.
We are all in agreement. The minister was here, but he' was behind the curtain and I did not know he was there.
Don't spoil your retreat.

Mr. Speaker, I hope that clears up this situation.
I was dealing particularly with the speech of the Minister of Agriculture this afternoon.

As he reviewed the history of this project throughout the years he said, among other things, that never had he promised to proceed with this project. I have before me the report of a speech made by him on June 23, 1949, as contained in the Regina Leader-Post. In the report of this speech delivered at Lemberg on that date-which Your Honour will remember was a few days before the election -the following appears:
The South Saskatchewan project would provide power and encourage building of industries in small towns, provide an incentive for young people to stay in this province. "I think we have made a fairly good start now," said Mr. Gardiner; "send us back to complete the job."
Since that promise was given, what has been done to finish the job? In 1948 the question arose in the house as to the need of money for the purpose of proceeding with the investigation into the feasibility of the project. In 1949 the matter came before the house following the election of that year, and at page 772 of Hansard the following appears:
If the South Saskatchewan river project was built under conditions that existed some three or four years ago it would cost in the neighbourhood of $60 million.
That is the Minister of Agriculture speaking. Then:
What would it cost today?

If it had to be built under conditions as they are today that amount would be increased by perhaps $10 million or maybe a little more. Eut it would be absolutely impossible to construct the South Saskatchewan river project in less than ten years. The total expenditure required would be averaged out over that period of time at somewhere between $6 million and $8 million per year.
Then again, a little later on, at page 773-
That is at the time my friends over here were accusing me of not going to build it at all.

Yes; that is correct. As reported at page 773 of Hansard the minister said:
Members of the committee and of the house asked the same questions then-
That is when the estimates were up for consideration.
-as are being asked now and tried to force the government to take the position that we were going to proceed with construction. We said that it was necessary to spend another $2 million before we could make a definite decision on the question whether we should proceed with construction.
That promise was unqualified. Parliament voted that money. It was expended. This was in October, 1949. The expenditure was made and the P.F.R.A. engineers determined the feasibility of this project; and from then on every type of roadblock has been thrown in the way of the project.
South Saskatchewan River Project
Then in 1951 the matter came up for consideration again. It came before the house, and at that time there were some references to the promises that had been made and in particular to the promises made in the Rosthern by-election, which goes back to 1948. On October 22, 1948, Mr. Tucker, who is now leader of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan, spoke on this subject and said:
He added, "You certainly won't get anywhere by sending C.C.F.ers to Ottawa: the election of Makaroff would be tantamount to repudiation of the great scheme."
Mr. Makaroff was a C.C.F. candidate. I continue:
"We have now reached the stage where public opinion will have to be mobilized behind the project to help obtain the passage through parliament of the necessary funds." Mr. Tucker continued, "it is imperative for the people of Rosthern to send Mr. Boucher to Ottawa to help Mr. Gardiner in his fight for it."
No politics in it.

Well, I have heard nothing from Mr. Boucher on that subject lately. He was sent down here for the purpose of showing parliament that this scheme had to be proceeded with. Then came 1951, and in giving his support to this proposition the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said at page 938 of Hansard:
1 was convinced before we started that we ought to find something that would be absolutely satisfactory. I have been trying to find it for the past sixteen years, and personally I am satisfied it has been found. But I am quite sure that every member of this house would agree that when it comes to proposing to spend $68 million out of the treasury of Canada we should at least ask three men who are experts to examine the records upon which I have based my opinion, and upon which others have based theirs, and to say whether or not they agree with it.
When the commission was set up, its purpose was to examine the reports and ascertain whether or not the engineers and the officials of P.F.R.A. had come to a proper decision. Is there any word in the English language, Mr. Speaker, that will describe what actually happened? With a commission set up for the purpose of examining what had or had not been done by the officials of P.F.R.A. over the years, we have something that is almost impossible to understand. As I remember it the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said the other day the reason we did not have the P.F.R.A. officials appear before the commission was that these men were government officials and they did not want to place them in a position of having to make recommendations to the government as to what should be done.

If the hon. member would permit me; I am sure he wants to be fair, and that is not all I said. I said that the

South Saskatchewan River Project commissioners had available to them all the information that had been gathered by the P.F.R.A. officials; that what we wanted from the commissioners was further information and not opinions of our own officials and that we did not think it would be proper to have them go and express their opinions when we were asking this commission to give us further information and to give us their opinions so that we might form our own.

Well, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has set out what he said on that occasion in summary form. In view of the fact that he is here on this occasion I should like him to answer this question. In view of the fact that we in western Canada and in the province of Saskatchewan are united in regard to the feasibility of this project and the necessity of going ahead with it, may I bring to his attention the demand of the people in western Canada in that regard and ask him now whether or not, having regard to the report which has been before us, he intends through his government and with his government to give us that which we ask for?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The house is not in committee, Mr. Speaker, and it is quite irregular to ask questions; but I would not like to have the hon. gentleman go out and say that he had asked me a question and I failed to answer him. If the house will give me unanimous consent to answer I shall be glad to do so.
You have it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The government is not prepared to go ahead, without further information, to recommend to parliament the expenditure of the amounts estimated by the commissioners, and will not take it upon itself to do that until it has further information.
What is the further information?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The further information is as to whether or not this is the best use to be made of that great national asset. Personally I think that it is a good use to be made of it, and if I can be convinced to the extent where I can honestly say that I believe it to be the best, I will recommend to my colleagues to make the recommendation to parliament. But I want to be sure that if this asset is used in this way it will not be apparent shortly afterward that there was a better use to which it should have been put.
What proof is required for that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Well, the commissioners say there has not yet been sufficient investigation to enable them to say that this is the best use. I do not know of any better use. But they suggest-and they are experts, I am not-that that further information is required to reach a positive opinion as to whether or not that is the best use. I think it would be a good use. I am not frightened at the cost. We anticipated that in the years 1952 and 1953 the cost would necessarily be higher than what had been estimated a few years ago. And the part of the cost that would be an expense to the federal treasury is nothing of the order of $250 million. The $250 million is made up of some elements which would not be at the expense of the federal treasury. Nevertheless the project is one of great magnitude, and it is one that will have to be accepted by the whole of Canada as a good, reasonable project to undertake. Had there not been the suggestion in the report that it was quite possible there might be a better use to be made of that great national asset I would have continued in the opinion that the creation of that body of water in the province of Saskatchewan would be a magnificent thing, and that the indirect, not the direct returns-the direct returns you cannot calculate mathematically -would be a permanent addition to the capital value of this great country of ours.

We are making advances as we proceed, Mr. Speaker. That is a long way farther than the Prime Minister or anyone connected with the government has gone previously; and before I deal with what he had to say-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That, Mr. Speaker, is not quite fair. I made that statement in the province of Saskatchewan in 1949, before the dissolution of parliament.

Yes, Mr. Speaker; the Prime Minister spoke in Saskatoon in 1949, and in every sentence he uttered he gave complete approval to the proposition and left the indication with the people of Saskatchewan that if his party were returned the project would be proceeded with.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No; that is quite wrong. I will not at this time, any more than I did at that time, make representations that I do not firmly believe in.

I say that the Prime Minister in 1949 offered only one veto, and that was the fear that Saskatoon would suffer what happened to Sodom and Gomorrah, the only difference being that in one case it was going to be by water and in the other case by fire. In 1949 the Prime Minister left the

impression-and every Liberal candidate in Saskatchewan was pledged and pledged the government-that this proposition would be gone ahead with.
Finally, after the election was over, the procrastination commenced. First they set up the water board. They did not know whether or not the water could be properly allocated as between the provinces. Having set up the water board, the next point raised was that the responsibility for irrigation should rest on the province. The attitude of the government was that as far as irrigation was concerned that responsibility would have to be accepted by the province of Saskatchewan. The province of Saskatchewan accepted that responsibility.
The next escape hatch was to set up a royal commission. When, over and over again, I asked in the house whether, if the royal commission report was favourable, the work would be proceeded with, the answer invariably was the same, that no such binding undertaking would be given. I could quote repetitious cases over and over again of statements in that regard.
And now we come to 1953. After the royal commission has sat for over a year, and we are unable to have any kind of assurance, there is to be some other investigation. First it was going to be proceeded with, we were told, in 1948, provided the feasibility were determined by P.F.R.A. They determined that.
Only a few moments ago the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said I had misquoted what he had said regarding the use of officials of P.F.R.A. I made the statement that the Prime Minister left the impression by his answer and actually said, in effect, that the reason these P.F.R.A. officials were not before the royal commission, and their report examined by the royal commission, was because of 'the danger that they, being civil servants, would be in the position of advising the government, of which they are the servants.
Well, I was not very far out in my interpretation of the answer given by the Prime Minister as it appears at page 1399 of Hansard for January 28, 1953, where the Prime Minister said:
This commission was established to get information which the government did not already have and to make recommendations to it. As the commissioners had access to all the records and technical advice of the P.F.R.A., it was not necessary for them to have formal appearances by federal officials at public hearings. The government shared this view and gave this opinion to the officials of the P.F.R.A.
In reaching that conclusion, the government had in mind the fact that it would not be fair to place civil servants in a false position by requiring them
South Saskatchewan River Project to appear publicly and express opinions on matters on which the Minister of Agriculture and the government as a whole had subsequently to reach decisions.
And that is exactly, in effect, what I said a while ago.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is in effect what the hon. member said. But it is not in effect the whole of what I said.

I have read every part of the discussion relative to civil servants in the answer the Prime Minister gave on that occasion. I, for one, for the life of me cannot understand why, over and over again, as we approach each election-1945, 1949 and 1953-we always find ourselves in the position of having this project just around the corner. Surely there is enough information for the government as to the feasibility. The location of the dam was finally determined in 1949 or 1950. Those of us in the province of Saskatchewan know what great benefits would flow from this development. Throughout the years we have given support to people in other parts of Canada in connection with projects national in scope that, through the years, will shape a prosperity hitherto not known, and will pay dividends in national development the like of which today we can only envisage.
We want this done. We want this work proceeded with. We have been promised it through the years. It has been dangled at each election as a bait, and after each election it has been withdrawn by postponement, by procrastination, by roadblocks and other interference.
This afternoon the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) used words that can only be interpreted to mean that the cabinet has not yet made any decision, as the matter has not been presented to them. I say that surely, after all these years, the cabinet knows and envisages the situation as it is. I think the time has come to take drastic action. In 1949, in order to demand their rights, the farmers of western Canada had to send a delegation to Ottawa. I think the time has come, in the national interest, when representatives from Saskatchewan, not only of the association connected with the project itself but of municipalities and rural areas throughout central Saskatchewan, will have to come in a delegation to parliament. They will have to send here a delegation charged with placing before the cabinet that about which not only the Minister of Agriculture but also members from Saskatchewan supporting the government have not as yet been able to impress the cabinet.
