Any farmer who happens to have land along the 400 miles of the shore line of that lake will be able to irrigate anywhere from 50 to 100 acres. What will they do? They will build up herds of livestock because they will be able to grow feed. In western Canada we are all anxious to have feed, especially those who live in the dried-out areas. When you produce livestock and livestock products they will be marketed throughout Canada. As our population grows we will be able to utilize this irrigated land.
I am not going to go into the details of what the land will produce, but I should like to say a few words with regard to the report of this commission. When the people in eastern Canada look at the report and see that $250 million may have to be spent in central Saskatchewan, they naturally come to the conclusion that that is a lot of money. If a report were to come out that the St. Lawrence development was to cost half a billion dollars, there would be a hubbub and cry all over eastern Canada. But that half billion dollars would not be spent in one year; it might take ten, fifteen or twenty years to spend it.
The same thing is true of the South Saskatchewan water development scheme. We are not asking that all this money be spent on this dam in one year, we are asking that it be spent over a period of years. If it takes six, eight or ten years to spend $100 million that is at the rate of $8 or $10 million a year. That is not asking for too much from the people of Canada in order to develop this area.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) told us this afternoon that the South Saskatchewan river project, and particularly the South Saskatchewan dam, had not been discussed in the cabinet, I confess that I could hardly believe it. But tonight, after listening to the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) which he interjected during the course of the speech made by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), I am inclined to believe that at least there has not been sufficient discussion of this matter in the cabinet itself. As a matter of fact, if there has been discussion they do not seem to have cleared with each other so as to be able to say the same thing on the floor of the House of Commons.
The Minister of Agriculture tried to suggest this afternoon that the item in the estimates
[Mr. Ferried

is one which could be used, if the cabinet so decided, to go ahead with the construction of the South Saskatchewan dam. Certainly that was an attempt on the part of the Minister of Agriculture to say that the hope which the people of Saskatchewan have that this dam will be built is one they can count on being fulfilled in the not far distant future. But tonight the Prime Minister stands up and says in clear-cut language that in the light of the figures now before him-* I do not know whether or not they are before the cabinet but they are before him-in this latest report he is not now prepared to recommend to the cabinet the vote of the necessary money to go ahead with this project.

On a question of privilege, I should like to say that I have never said any such thing as my hon. friend has just tried to indicate. I have never said any such thing at all. I have never said anything different from what the Prime Minister said. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

I am glad to know that is the way the member for Springfield feels with regard to the incident in 1946, and I accept his word on it without question. As a result of that considerable body of opinion being expressed on the government side, led in this instance by the member for Springfield and supported by the member for


Fraser Valley and by the only private member from Saskatchewan at that time, Mr. Walter Tucker, the government took quite a different stand from that which is being taken in this debate. On that occasion the present Prime Minister, who was then acting prime minister in the absence of Mr. King, did his best to persuade the house to allow the amendment to be withdrawn on the assurance that the government would give consideration to the matter. We were not prepared to withdraw the amendment, so a little later the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) who was then the minister of reconstruction and supply, got up and said as recorded on page 5431 of Hansard:
Nevertheless the government has no objection to an expression of opinion from the members of the house. I suggest that the vote should be a free expression regardless of party.
He went on to say:
The difficulty of obtaining the expression arises from the form of the amendment, which in itself denies the right of the house to move into committee of supply at this time. However, Mr. Speaker, I would call to your attention article 489 of Beauchesne, which reads as follows:
When an amendment has been adopted to the motion for the house to go into committee of supply or of ways and means, it may be forthwith moved that the house resolve itself into such committee immediately or on a future day.
Immediately after quoting that rule from Beauchesne the then minister of reconstruction and supply said:
Therefore I should like to serve notice that if this vote carries the government will immediately move that the house go into committee of supply this day. I believe that that procedure is consistent with the rules, and if there can be general agreement on that point the work of the house can be facilitated and the objective of hon. members attained.
Well, the result was that not only courageous members, like the hon. member for Springfield and the hon. member for Fraser Valley and others who had already indicated their support, voted for our amendment, but when the vote was called at least twenty Liberal members joined with most of those on the opposition side of the house. The result was that the amendment to the motion to go into supply was carried by a vote of 69 to 41.
Was it a vote of [DOT] non-confidence in the government? No. That had already been made clear by the announcement of the present Minister of Trade and Commerce. As a result of his announcement, and as a result of the notice he had given, immediately after that amendment had been carried and had thus became an expression of opinion of the house, the present Prime Minister got up and moved "that the house do now go into committee of supply". About half

a column down in Hansard that motion was agreed to and the house went into committee of supply and went on with its business.

1. The commission finds that at present the economic returns to the Canadian people on the mvestment in the proposed South Saskatchewan
Mr. Knowles.]

river project (central Saskatchewan development) are not commensurate with the cost thereof; though the project would yield social returns which, while they cannot be measured for the purpose of this report, would be of great value to the region in which it is situated.

I think the government in its wisdom has taken great precautions in going ahead with this land irrigation scheme which is estimated to cost anywhere from $100 million to $350 million. If they did not have the backing of every party in this house they would be accused later on of making a terrible mistake. Therefore I think the government are wise in taking these steps to make sure that every hon. member is behind this huge proposition before that large amount of money is spent.
At present there are large surpluses of wheat in Canada, and there is no shortage of food. There is no great hurry for such a project at this time. Mr. Speaker, the discussion I have listened to this afternoon and this evening from the opposition side of the house indicates to me that the South Saskatchewan project, as far as they are concerned, has been relegated to the position of a political football. The two amendments to the motion to go into supply that are now before the house are indicative of that. The movers of those motions propose that we should support their amendments and thereby, as Liberals from Saskatchewan, show our faith in the dam on the South Saskatchewan river. As anyone knows, notwithstanding the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), a motion to go into supply is made for the purpose of voting money to Her Majesty's government to carry on the work of the government. If the government is defeated on that motion it ceases to be in power and we must have an immediate election.
Are you afraid of that?

Just a minute; I see in these amendments a double-barrelled gun, as it were. In one case it is supposed to put the Liberal members from Saskatchewan on their mettle and at a disadvantage. On the other hand, if the amendment is adopted it puts the government out of office. If history tells us anything, it tells us that all major projects in this country have been dealt with and put into effect by this government. I am not much interested in a project that would put this government out of office and would put some other one in that we would have to depend on to put the South Saskatchewan river project into effect.
In all the speeches so far from the other side of the house I have not heard anything to bolster the argument for a South Saskatchewan dam. We have a report here, which fortunately has not been stolen, that casts a lot of doubt on the advisability of the South Saskatchewan project as an economic proposition. I would think hon. members opposite could make better use of their talents, if they are honestly in favour of this dam and not in embarrassing Liberals-which I can assure them they are not doing-by trying 68108-114
South Saskatchewan River Project to balance up some of the criticism that is to be found in this report.
I gathered from the minister's remarks this afternoon and from some other information I have obtained that it would be appropriate to sell this project to the people of Canada. When the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Ferrie) dealt with that angle of the proposition my hon. friends laughed, but they know as well as anybody that we have to sell this proposition to the people of Canada on an economic basis. This is one possible way of doing it. If you take the figures the minister gave this afternoon you will find that we have paid out a lot of money in Saskatchewan by way of rehabilitation in the dried-out period, that bad economic time we went through, on account of the dry years. We are pouring a lot of money into a pail that perhaps has a hole in the bottom.
Just what have we spent in rehabilitating the west that could be used to put this proposition on an economic basis, a proposition that is going to pay for itself? We have to do that or show the people of Canada that they are going to save some money by putting in the dam. I think we can show them that we are going to save some money. We have spent $135 million in prairie farm assistance payments, of which the farmer has paid some $52 million, leaving $83 million that the federal government has put out in prairie farm assistance. We have spent $168 million in direct relief in the west in the dried-out period. We have spent another $39 million on prairie farm rehabilitation in small projects; we have spent a further $22 million on large projects such as the St. Mary dam and the Bow river project, the last mostly in Alberta. In all that is $312 million that we have spent on rehabilitation. You would not have to dig very far to find out that we have spent more than that. If we are to spend $312 million every fifteen or twenty years in rehabilitation would it not be better to put a lake in that dry area and irrigate, as this South Saskatchewan project calls for?
I do not know why I should be talking for the province of Saskatchewan, particularly as I happen to be in a section where we are not lacking water. I just happened to bring down a few maps of some parts of my riding. These are air maps. As hon. members can see, there is just about as much water in this area as there is land. Each one of these areas is a small portion of the riding. As you go through this country you see that there is plenty of water. In fact there is more water in my riding than will fill this

South Saskatchewan River Project particular project a thousand times; therefore we are not exactly dry in some parts of Saskatchewan.
This particular project will have no impact upon the riding of Meadow Lake, except that we may get some power from it. It is odd that these amendments should have been moved by members of opposition groups from Saskatchewan, and it is worthy of note that there has not been any opposition shown by the group from Alberta. They are not interested in playing politics with this issue, because they have had some irrigation in their province and they know the value of it. We are thankful to them for the way they have approached this matter.
I think there is some difference of opinion between the people of Saskatchewan and those of Alberta as to who should have most of the water. That is only natural. It is natural to suppose that they want to keep in Alberta as much of the water as they possibly can. They know the value of it, just as we do. But, Mr. Speaker, in the southern part of the province-from which I do not come- they definitely do need this dam. In view of the water we have in my constituency, I am in the same position as someone in the eastern part of Canada who is not directly connected with this project at all.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) has said that he has been disappointed in the stand taken by Liberals from Saskatchewan. I can reciprocate his feelings entirely and say that I am disappointed in the action his group are taking in this matter. They are making the South Saskatchewan dam a political football. If that is what they want to do, well and good; but it will not get us a dam. We had better say to the people of Canada that this is an economically sound proposition, and sell it to them on that basis. If it is an economically sound proposition, then it will save that amount of money in the next twenty or thirty years, and we will not have to pour so many millions of dollars into the province.
We will not have to do it all at one time, either. As the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Ferrie) has pointed out, it will be carried out on a ten-year or twelve-year basis, and would cost about $10 million a year. As members of the house representing the people of Canada we have to show that this is an economically sound proposition. We realize that while hon. members in the opposition were shouting only a short time ago that they are all in favour of this project, the fact is that they still have to go back home and sell it to their constituents. There is no reason why that cannot be done.

I just wish to indicate my position. So far as I am concerned, when my friends opposite move amendments which, if carried, would put the government out of office, I must definitely oppose them. I would not mind if we had an election tomorrow, but I most definitely am opposed to going out in that manner, bowing to a minority which 1 am sure will still be a minority after the next election.
And so, Mr. Speaker, I will have great pleasure in voting against the amendments, especially in the light of the spirit in which they are put forward. If they would accomplish anything toward getting the dam, 1 would be very pleased to support them. But they are not going to accomplish anything. Hon. members know that, and they knew it when the amendments were moved. I will have great pleasure in voting against the amendments on these grounds.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say only a few words tonight before ten o'clock.
Move the adjournment. It is ten o'clock.

I will do that when I get ready. I think I should say a few words before the vote is taken on the amendment and the subamendment. The debate started out as a discussion of the dam, and now it has developed into a discussion of the vote.
I want to assure my hon. friends to my left that if I thought for one moment that voting for the amendment or the subamendment would get the dam, there would be no question about how I would vote.
It might help.

You say it
might help. Well, we can take a look at that, too. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has indicated that a decision has not been made, and the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has said the same thing.
I think the government would be as seriously criticized by the opposition-I have said "I think"; I shall correct that by saying "I am sure"-if a decision were reached at this moment by the cabinet, without giving further consideration to the report. I have not much use for commissions because I feel-and I am becoming more convinced all the time-that they are used only for political advantage. That has been my impression since I have come here.
Who appointed the commission?

Those of us who are not in favour of the wording of the

commission's report are condemning it. However, it was mentioned tonight-I believe it was the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Ferrie) who made the suggestion-that members in the opposition, including the hon member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), might very well discuss this matter with the various ministers.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has said that this has not been discussed in cabinet. I take his word for that. But privately I have discussed this matter with each cabinet minister, and tried to suggest the importance of it to our province. As you know, caucus is something that is secret; at the same time I do not think I would be breaking any rule if I were to say that this project was definitely discussed in government caucus. I myself brought it up. What was said I am not privileged to repeat. However, speaking on this subject with the Prime Minister himself, privately, I tried to suggest that, so far as the federal government was concerned, we would be responsible for only part of the dam. The Prime Minister reminded me that although the federal government would be responsible for only part, the government would still be respon-
South Saskatchewan River Project sible for taxes even in the province of Saskatchewan. If a dam is built, two-thirds of the cost being provided by the federal government and one-third by other means, the fact remains that it must be paid for out of taxes.

Ten o'clock.
On motion of Mr. Smith (Moose Mountain) the debate was adjourned.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow we shall continue consideration of the motion to go into supply, and call the following departments: external affairs, transport, labour, agriculture and justice. Then the Secretary of State for External Affairs will move to refer his estimates to the standing committee on external affairs. If we dispose of that motion we will take up the resolution in the name of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) respecting the Farm Improvement Loans Act, 1944, and then Bill No. 46, to amend the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, February 10, 1953
